# Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions

Coordinate `EN-113-000-0000-2-2026-PR-T4-UK-EX-M1-B-AL-H-0319` | `PM-159.1` | status ACTIVE | original slug `Quasipolynomial-Bounds-for-Arithmetic-Progressions-September-23-2026` | date 2026-09-23 | derived from the openai/math preprint Quasipolynomial-Bounds-for-Arithmetic-Progressions-September-23-2026, modified (Apache-2.0). <!-- PM:BEGIN pm.node.v2 -->
```json
{
  "abstract_verbatim": "We prove Erdős's conjecture that every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. More quantitatively, for every fixed <i>k</i> ≥ 3, we show\n\n$`\\displaystyle r_k(N)\\le C_kN\\exp\\bigl(-c_k(\\log N)^{\\varepsilon_k}\\bigr)`$\n\nwith $`C_k,c_k,\\varepsilon_k\\gt 0`$, where $`r_k(N)`$ is the largest size of a subset of $`\\{1,\\ldots,N\\}`$ with no nonconstant <i>k</i>-term arithmetic progression.",
```

<a id="pm-s1"></a>
## 1. Abstract and result contract

> We prove Erdős's conjecture that every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. More quantitatively, for every fixed <i>k</i> ≥ 3, we show
> 
> $`\displaystyle r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr)`$
> 
> with $`C_k,c_k,\varepsilon_k\gt 0`$, where $`r_k(N)`$ is the largest size of a subset of $`\{1,\ldots,N\}`$ with no nonconstant <i>k</i>-term arithmetic progression.

- **ap-main** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-main)): For each fixed integer $k\ge3$ there are constants $C_k,c_k,\varepsilon_k>0$ such that, for every $N\ge2$, $$\label{ap:density-bound} r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr).$$ Equivalently, there is $A_k\ge1$ such that an $\alpha$-dense subset of $[N]$ contains a nonconstant $k$-term progression whenever $$\label{ap:threshold} \log N\ge A_k\bigl(2+\log(1/\alpha)\bigr)^{A_k}, \qquad 0<\alpha\le1.$$
  - Explanation: Bounds the size of progression-free subsets of an interval and gives the equivalent density threshold.
- **ap-reciprocal** (theorem, [source](#stmt-ap-reciprocal)): Every set $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{a\in A}a^{-1}=\infty$ contains nonconstant arithmetic progressions of every finite length.
  - Explanation: Divergence of the reciprocal sum forces nonconstant progressions of every finite length.
- **ap-increment** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ap-increment)): There are fixed $D=D_k$, $\eta=\eta_k>0$, and polynomials with degrees depending only on $k$ having the following property. Suppose $p\ge2$, $a\ge e^{-p}$, and a progression-free input on a positive-dimensional integer box has a certificate <a href="#ap:certificate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ap:certificate">[ap:certificate]</a>, with width logs $Q_h=\log(2/w_h)$. If every root side is sufficiently large with logarithmic cutoff polynomial in $p$, the dimension data, and all $Q_h$, then either the hypotheses are impossible or a root slice carries a new certificate at threshold $(1+\eta)a$.* *The new cell retains the determining data through exact integer reparametrizations and adds at most $d_0=(2+p)^{C_k}$ fresh absolute slots together with downward preparation copies. Its dimensions $d'_i$ and width logs $Q'_i$ satisfy $$\begin{aligned} d'_i-d_i &\le d_0+P_i(p,d_{i+1},\ldots,d_D),\label{ap:dimension-rule}\\ Q'_i-Q_i &\le P'_i(p,\text{all dimension forecasts},Q_{i+1},\ldots,Q_D). \label{ap:width-rule} \end{aligned}$$ The root slice cost has polynomial logarithmic bound in all the same data, now including every $Q_i$. Polynomial exponents and the fixed gain are independent of the number of increments. Gap and discount choices can be made in advance from the dimension and cut-count forecasts.
  - Explanation: Returns an improved density certificate while preserving old determining data and controlling losses by strictly higher weights.
- **ap-absolute** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ap-absolute)): There are $\xi>0$ and $C=C_k$ with the following property. Let $p\ge2$, and let $f$ be a progression-free $[0,1]$-valued function of mean at least $a\ge e^{-p}$ on a box of positive dimension $n$. Suppose every side is sufficiently large, with a sufficient logarithmic cutoff polynomial in $2+p+n$. Then, unless the hypotheses are impossible, $f$ admits a degree-$s$ polynomial patch on a slice with positive score at target $(1+\xi)a$. The number of slots is at most $d_0=(2+p)^C$, independent of $n$. The logarithms of inverse score, Lipschitz norm, slice cost, and sufficient side cutoff are polynomial in $2+p+n$.
  - Explanation: The absolute increment adds a bounded fresh rank independently of the dimension; the other costs may depend on dimension.
- **ap-major-preparation** (construction, [source](#stmt-ap-major-preparation)): Given a triangular two-box certificate, forecast dimension bounds and descending numerical budgets in the sense of Definition <a href="#ap:budgets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:budgets">5</a>. After polynomially many rank-cut transactions, there is a certificate with an arbitrarily small prescribed total proportional target discount such that every rank-stop probability in the actual current sampling procedure is at most its prescribed bound. The procedure may restart its tests after every transaction.* *The dimensions added at block $i$ are polynomial in the dimensions strictly above $i$. The increase in its width logarithm is polynomial in dimension data, $p$, and higher-level numerical budgets, and is independent of its own initial width logarithm except for carrying that logarithm additively. Root slice costs and sufficient root-side cutoffs have polynomial logarithms in the full eventual budgets.
  - Explanation: Rank cuts prepare the sampling procedure while keeping dimension and precision dependence triangular.
- **ap-iteration-dimensions** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-iteration-dimensions)): For one round, the increase in the dimension of weight $i$ is bounded by $d_0$ plus a fixed polynomial in the incoming dimensions strictly above $i$. The number of preparation cuts and all structural variable counts are polynomial in the incoming dimensions and $p$. For a proposed run of $T=O_k(1+p)$ rounds on an interval, starting without slots, all these quantities admit polynomial bounds in $2+p$, chosen before any numerical precision.
  - Explanation: Structural forecasts bound dimension growth before numerical accuracies are chosen.
- **ap-iteration-widths** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-iteration-widths)): The choices above can be made with fixed polynomial logarithmic bounds. They give, in one round, $$\label{ap:iteration:width-rec} Q_j^{\rm out}\le q_j+P_j(p,d_*,q_{>j}).$$ where $P_j$ is a fixed polynomial independent of $q_j$ and of all lower width logs. The total root logarithmic slice loss and the sufficient root log-side cutoff are polynomial in $p,d_*$ and all incoming width logs. For the interval run of $O_k(1+p)$ rounds in Proposition <a href="#ap:iteration:dimensions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:iteration:dimensions">39</a>, starting without slots and with trivial width data, these width logs and the sums of root costs are polynomial in $2+p$.
  - Explanation: Descending width recurrences yield polynomial bounds on interval losses through the reserved run.
- **ap-iteration-closure** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-iteration-closure)): There are constants $C_k>0$ and $A_k\ge1$ such that a progression-free subset of $[N]$ of density $\alpha>0$ cannot satisfy $$\log N\ge C_k\bigl(2+\log(1/\alpha)\bigr)^{A_k}.$$
  - Explanation: The density increment process cannot sustain a progression-free set beyond the stated interval threshold.
- **ap-weighted-dyadic** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-weighted-dyadic)): For $w:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)$, set $$S_k(w)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}r_k(2^m) \max_{2^m\le n<2^{m+1}}w(n).$$ If $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ contains no nonconstant $k$-term progression, then $$\sum_{a\in A}w(a)\le S_k(w).$$ Consequently, whenever $S_k(w)<\infty$, divergence of the weighted sum forces a nonconstant $k$-term progression.
  - Explanation: Dyadic interval bounds transfer progression-free cardinality estimates to nonnegative weighted sums.
- **ap-weighted-harmonic** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-weighted-harmonic)): There is $H_k<\infty$ such that every $k$-term-progression-free $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1a\le H_k.$$ One may take $H_k=\sum_{m\ge0}2^{-m}r_k(2^m)$.
  - Explanation: The harmonic sum is uniformly bounded over sets avoiding a fixed progression length.
- **ap-weighted-stretched** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-weighted-stretched)): Every $k$-term-progression-free set has a uniformly bounded sum for each of the weights $$\begin{aligned} w_a(n)&=\frac{\exp(a(\log n)^\varepsilon)}{n}, &&0<a<c,\\ w_{*,\eta}(n)&= \frac{\exp(c(\log n)^\varepsilon)} {n\log n\,(\log\log n)^{1+\eta}}, &&\eta>0. \end{aligned}$$ The bound may depend on $k$ and the displayed parameters. Divergence for either weight therefore forces a nonconstant $k$-term progression.
  - Explanation: Larger weights still have uniformly bounded sums over progression-free sets in the specified parameter ranges.
- **ap-weighted-logarithmic** (theorem, [source](#stmt-ap-weighted-logarithmic)): For every fixed $B\ge0$, if $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac{(\log(2+a))^B}{a}=\infty,$$ then $A$ contains nonconstant arithmetic progressions of every finite length.
  - Explanation: A divergent logarithmically weighted reciprocal sum forces progressions of every finite length.
- **ap-weighted-tail** (bound, [source](#stmt-ap-weighted-tail)): There is $C'_k>0$ such that every $k$-term-progression-free set $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ satisfies, for all sufficiently large real $x$, $$\sum_{\substack{a\in A\\a>x}}\frac1a \le C'_k(\log x)^{1-\varepsilon_k} e^{-c_k(\log x)^{\varepsilon_k}}.$$ In particular, for every $0<a<c_k$, this tail is at most $C_{k,a}e^{-a(\log x)^{\varepsilon_k}}$.
  - Explanation: The harmonic mass above a large cutoff has a uniform stretched-exponential tail bound.
- **prelim-inverse** (theorem, [source](#stmt-prelim-inverse)): Fix an integer $s\ge1$. Let $p\ge2$. A unit-bounded function on an interval whose $U^{s+1}$ norm is at least $e^{-p}$ correlates by at least $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$ with a unit-bounded degree-$s$ niltest of complexity $\mathcal P(p)$. The same conclusion holds on integer boxes and on products of cyclic groups, with the following dimension convention: for every fixed $A\ge1$, dimension $n\le(2+p)^A$ is permitted, and the constants and polynomial exponents may depend only on $s,A$. On a product of cyclic groups the niltest is evaluated in the coordinatewise integer representatives.
  - Explanation: Large uniformity norm gives correlation with a controlled niltest, including the stated dimension convention.
- **counting-relative-target** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-counting-relative-target)): Fix $s\ge1$, put $k=s+2$, and fix a sufficiently large dimension $n_0=n_0(s)$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$. There is an exponent $E$, depending only on these fixed parameters, with the following property.* *Fix the side-comparability constant $R=2^{n_0+1}$. Let $p\geq2$, $e^{-p}\leq a\leq\Lambda\leq1$, and suppose an absolute rule holds on every sufficiently large prime-sided box of dimension $n_0$, with distinct sides and largest side at most $R$ times the smallest: every progression-free input of mean at least $a$ has, on a parameter slice of cost at most $p$, a degree-$s$ patch of rank at most $d_0$, complexity at most $p$, and score at least $e^{-p}$ against input minus $\Lambda$. The cutoff on every prime side is at most $e^p$.* *Let $Q$ be any box of dimension between $1$ and $p$, with all sides at least $\exp((2+p)^E)$. Suppose $0\leq f\leq1$ is progression-free on $Q$, and an old degree-$s$ patch $B$ of rank $d$ and complexity at most $p$ satisfies $$\mathbb E_Q(f-a)B\geq e^{-p}.$$ Then some parameter slice of $Q$, of cost at most $(2+p)^E$, carries a degree-$s$ patch $B'$ satisfying $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{rank}}B'&\leq d+d_0,\\ \text{complexity}(B')&\leq(2+p)^E,\\ \mathbb E\bigl(f-(1-\varepsilon_0)\Lambda\bigr)B' &\geq\exp(-(2+p)^E). \end{aligned}$$ There is also a separate impossibility alternative: if $e^{-p}\leq a\leq1$ and the absolute rule states that no such input of mean at least $a$ exists, the old positive score is impossible. This alternative has no target parameter $\Lambda$. The exponent is independent of the absolute rule, of $d,d_0$, and of every variable dimension included in $p$.
  - Explanation: A uniform absolute rule lifts to an old patch with additive rank, with a separate impossibility alternative.
- **lifting-linear-rank** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lifting-linear-rank)): Assume the following three assertions, with their permitted early or augmented logarithmic cost bounds:* 1. *rank preparation and conditioned sampling remove the lowest $D$ slots of weight $j$, retaining positive absolute score and producing spaces with $\sum_h\dim W_h\le D$;* 2. *a family of recursively returned patches of rank at most $d_*$ can be globalized in the same patch group as in Proposition <a href="#lifting:candidate-globalization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lifting:candidate-globalization">115</a>;* 3. *transferring this fixed global patch to the parent costs at most $\sum_h\dim W_h$ new slots, and uses an arbitrarily prescribed fixed multiplicative discount of the target density.* *Assume also the unconditioned base case returns rank at most $d_0$ and permits an arbitrarily prescribed fixed density discount. Then processing an old patch with $d$ slots returns rank at most $d_0+d$. For fixed $s$, its total multiplicative density discount can be made at most any prescribed $\epsilon_0>0$.
  - Explanation: Recursive removal of old slots accounts for the returned rank additively.
- **lifting-relative-theorem** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lifting-relative-theorem)): Assume Lemmas <a href="#prelim:step-drop" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:step-drop">56</a> and <a href="#prelim:separation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:separation">51</a>, Proposition <a href="#sampling:constrained" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:constrained">[sampling:constrained]</a>, and the scalar transfer of Proposition <a href="#sampling:scalar-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:scalar-transfer">78</a>, including their stated uniform polynomial logarithmic bounds. Then Proposition <a href="#counting:relative-target" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="counting:relative-target">76</a> holds, with rank at most $d_0+d$ in its increment alternative. Its exponent $E$ depends only on $s$, the fixed base dimension $n_0$, its fixed side-ratio bound, and the prescribed discount $\varepsilon_0$.
  - Explanation: The stated sampling and symbol assertions imply relative lifting with additive rank and uniform logarithmic bounds.

```json
        "exact_quote": "Given a triangular two-box certificate, forecast dimension bounds and descending numerical budgets in the sense of Definition <a href=\"#ap:budgets\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"ap:budgets\">5</a>. <a id="pm-s2"></a>
```
## 2. Definitions, validity and bounds

- **Progression-free extremal cardinality** ([source](#ap:introduction)): For integers $k\ge3$ and $N\ge1$, let $r_k(N)$ be the largest cardinality of a subset of $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing no nonconstant $k$-term arithmetic progression $a,a+d,\ldots,a+(k-1)d$, with $d>0$.
- **Coloring threshold** ([source](#pm-h-8)): Let $W_r(k)$ be the least integer $N$ such that every coloring of $[N]$ with $r$ colors contains a monochromatic nonconstant $k$-term arithmetic progression.
- **Triangular cell** ([source](#pm-h-12)): A triangular cell is specified by polynomials $$C_h(u,b_{<h})\in\mathbb R^{d_h},\qquad \deg_{\rm wt}C_h\le h,$$ bounded centers $l_h$, and widths $0<w_h\le1/32$.
- **Logarithmic width precision** ([source](#pm-h-12)): Put $$Q_h=\log(2/w_h).$$
- **Density certificate** ([source](#ap:certificate)): A *density certificate* is $$\label{ap:certificate} \mathbb EfB^- > a\mathbb EB^+, \qquad 0\le f\le1,$$ where $f$ is progression-free.
- **Polynomial patch** ([source](#ap:analytic-objects)): A degree-$q$ *patch* is $$\label{ap:patch-definition} B(u)=\sum_{b\in\mathbb Z^d}\Phi(S_u(b)),\qquad S_u(b)_i=b_i-A_i(u,b_1,\ldots,b_{i-1}),$$ where $\deg_{\rm wt}A_i\le\omega_i$ and $\Phi:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]$ is Lipschitz and supported in $[-1/4,1/4]^d$.
- **Warm data** ([source](#stmt-ap-budgets)): At layer $j$, the *warm data* consist of $p$, forecasts for all dimensions and structural variable counts, gap parameters depending only on these data, and the widths and numerical budgets already chosen at layers strictly above $j$.
- **Parameter slice** ([source](#stmt-counting-slice)): A parameter slice of an integer box is a subbox intersected with one coordinatewise residue class modulo a common positive integer, followed by affine reindexing as a box.
- **Niltest** ([source](#prelim:grids)): A degree-$s$ niltest is $t\mapsto F(g(t)\Gamma)$, where $F$ is bounded and Lipschitz for the quotient of the right-invariant Riemannian metric that makes the declared coordinate basis orthonormal at the identity.

<a id="pm-s3"></a>
## 3. Proof roadmap

- **prelim-inverse** [claim](#stmt-prelim-inverse) / [proof](#stmt-prelim-inverse): Correlate a uniformity obstruction with a controlled niltest. -> Structured correlation.
- **counting-relative-target** [claim](#stmt-counting-relative-target) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lifting-relative-theorem): Lift a uniform absolute rule with additive rank. -> Relative patch increment.
- **ap-absolute** [claim](#stmt-ap-absolute) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-absolute): Apply relative lifting to the constant old patch. -> Dimension-independent fresh rank.
- **ap-major-preparation** [claim](#stmt-ap-major-preparation) / [proof](#ap:preparation): Cut rank obstructions while preserving the certificate. -> Prepared cell.
- **ap-increment** [claim](#stmt-ap-increment) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-iteration-widths-2): Descend to terminal boxes and return the increment with exact determining equations. -> Improved triangular certificate.
- **ap-iteration-dimensions** [claim](#stmt-ap-iteration-dimensions) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-iteration-dimensions): Forecast structural dimensions before numerical precision. -> Polynomial structural forecast.
- **ap-iteration-widths** [claim](#stmt-ap-iteration-widths) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-iteration-widths): Choose descending precision bounds using only higher widths. -> Polynomial cumulative width costs.
- **ap-iteration-closure** [claim](#stmt-ap-iteration-closure) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-iteration-closure): Iterate until a certificate would exceed its density ceiling. -> Finite-horizon density obstruction.
- **ap-weighted-dyadic** [claim](#stmt-ap-weighted-dyadic) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-weighted-dyadic): Bound each dyadic interval by its extremal cardinality. -> Weighted summation bound.
- **ap-weighted-harmonic** [claim](#stmt-ap-weighted-harmonic) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-weighted-harmonic): Sum the dyadic density estimate with reciprocal weights. -> Uniform finite harmonic ceiling.
- **ap-weighted-logarithmic** [claim](#stmt-ap-weighted-logarithmic) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-weighted-logarithmic): Absorb fixed logarithmic weights into stretched-exponential decay. -> Divergence criterion for every length.
- **ap-weighted-tail** [claim](#stmt-ap-weighted-tail) / [proof](#proof-stmt-ap-weighted-tail): Compare the dyadic tail with a decaying integral. -> Uniform harmonic tail estimate.

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **I-DENSITY**: The progression-free density estimate is stated for each fixed progression length, with constants depending on that length.
- **I-JET**: The Boolean jet has a finite number of coordinates, and determines all vertex values.
- **I-ZERO**: The Boolean jet at cube order zero consists of a single value.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **A-VARIABLE**: Apply the density bound uniformly while the progression length varies. -> Dependence of the constants on progression length prevents that uniform conclusion.
- **A-CONVERSE**: Conclude that a convergent reciprocal sum excludes long progressions. -> The divergent-sum implication does not supply this converse.
- **A-JET**: Treat a Boolean-jet dimension check as a verification of progression density bounds. -> Counting coordinates does not establish the analytic density increment estimates.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `constructive`. The Boolean jet has a finite coordinate count obtained by reducing powers on the Boolean cube. This executable component checks that count; it does not certify the density theorem or its analytic inputs.

```python
# INPUTS: JSON list of [h,q] integer pairs.
# PRECONDITIONS: 1 <= h <= 5 and 0 <= q <= 4; booleans excluded.
# OUTPUTS: JSON list of exact Boolean-jet coordinate counts, in input order.
# TIME: O(sum(q * min(h,q))) exact integer additions.
# SPACE: O(max(min(h,q))) integer cells besides input and output.
# ARITHMETIC: python-flint fmpz exact integers; no floating point.
# FAILURE: invalid input raises ValueError and exits nonzero.
import json, sys
from flint import fmpz
pairs = json.load(sys.stdin)
if not isinstance(pairs, list) or not pairs:
    raise ValueError('nonempty list required')
answers = []
for pair in pairs:
    if not isinstance(pair, list) or len(pair) != 2:
        raise ValueError('pair required')
    h, q = pair
    if type(h) is not int or type(q) is not int or not (1 <= h <= 5 and 0 <= q <= 4):
        raise ValueError('outside checked contract')
    cap = min(h, q)
    row = [fmpz(1)] + [fmpz(0)] * cap
    for step in range(q):
        for degree in range(cap, 0, -1):
            row[degree] += row[degree - 1]
    answers.append(int(sum(row)))
print(json.dumps(answers))
```

```json
    "reference_code": "# INPUTS: JSON list of [h,q] integer pairs.\n# PRECONDITIONS: 1 <= h <= 5 and 0 <= q <= 4; booleans excluded.\n# OUTPUTS: JSON list of exact Boolean-jet coordinate counts, in input order.\n# TIME: O(sum(q * min(h,q))) exact integer additions.\n# SPACE: O(max(min(h,q))) integer cells besides input and output.\n# ARITHMETIC: python-flint fmpz exact integers; no floating point.\n# FAILURE: invalid input raises ValueError and exits nonzero.\nimport json, sys\nfrom flint import fmpz\npairs = json.load(sys.stdin)\nif not isinstance(pairs, list) or not pairs:\n    raise ValueError('nonempty list required')\nanswers = []\nfor pair in pairs:\n    if not isinstance(pair, list) or len(pair) != 2:\n        raise ValueError('pair required')\n    h, q = pair\n    if type(h) is not int or type(q) is not int or not (1 <= h <= 5 and 0 <= q <= 4):\n        raise ValueError('outside checked contract')\n    cap = min(h, q)\n    row = [fmpz(1)] + [fmpz(0)] * cap\n    for step in range(q):\n        for degree in range(cap, 0, -1):\n            row[degree] += row[degree - 1]\n    answers.append(int(sum(row)))\nprint(json.dumps(answers))\n",
    "test_vectors": [
      {

        "input": "[[1, 0]]"
      },

        "input": "[[1, 4]]"

        "input": "[[4, 4]]"
```

## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **L1** (hypothesis): The density bound is for each fixed progression length; dependence of the constants on that length is allowed. Uniform bounds for growing progression length are ABSENT. Blocked use: ['Using the same constants while the progression length grows with the interval.']
- **L2** (unknown): Numerical values for the density-bound constants are ABSENT from the theorem statement; a concrete threshold requires additional quantitative information. Blocked use: ['Reporting a numerical sufficient interval length from unspecified constants.']
- **L3** (hypothesis): The reciprocal-sum conclusion assumes divergence. Convergence alone yields no progression guarantee from this corollary. Blocked use: ['Applying the reciprocal-sum corollary solely because a set is infinite.']
- **L4** (counterexample_scope): A fixed power saving in the interval length is incompatible with the stated three-term lower bound. Blocked use: ['Replacing the stretched-exponential density saving by a fixed power saving in the interval length.']
- **L5** (hypothesis): Decay of progression-free density to zero alone is insufficient for the reciprocal-sum deduction; the argument needs dyadic summability. Blocked use: ['Replacing the summable density estimate by qualitative density decay in the reciprocal-sum proof.']
- **L6** (approximation): Exact independence belongs to the residue comparison law. The actual tilted law is only compared to it within the prescribed total variation error. Blocked use: ['Treating the actual tilted residues as exactly independent.']
- **L7** (approximation): The finite-residue statement does not authorize a joint comparison at the product of all tested primes, or conditional uniformity after fixing an exact real lift. Blocked use: ['Combining separate prime-power comparisons into an unrestricted product modulus.', 'Conditioning on an exact real lift and asserting uniform residues.']
- **L8** (hypothesis): Recursive budgets and sampler dimensions must precede late rank thresholds and prepared-space heights; allowing late precision dependence would make the requirement circular. Blocked use: ['Choosing recursive accuracy or structural sampling dimensions from eventual prepared-space heights.']
- **L9** (hypothesis): The relative lifting theorem is conditional on its stated sampling, separation, step-drop and scalar-transfer inputs, including uniform polynomial logarithmic bounds. Blocked use: ['Treating relative lifting as independent of the asserted uniformity of its analytic inputs.']
- **L10** (edge_case): The affine Boolean cube ideal statement assumes independent cube directions and positive homogeneous degree. Degenerate directions require a separate analysis. Blocked use: ['Applying the independent-direction cube ideal statement to collapsed cubes without checking its hypotheses.']
- **L11** (formal_scope): A finite calculation of Boolean jet dimensions concerns the algebraic coordinate count only. It does not certify the density theorem or the infinite reciprocal-sum consequence. Blocked use: ['Promoting a finite Boolean-jet check into verification of the full density-increment argument.']

Scope note of family 159 (`lean/docs/159.md`, verbatim):

> The following describes the scope of the Lean formalization related to the following accompanying paper(s):
>
> - [Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions](../../preprints/Quasipolynomial-Bounds-for-Arithmetic-Progressions-September-23-2026/paper.pdf)
>
> ## Scope
>
> Erdős's reciprocal-sum conjecture asks whether every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The formalization proves this statement: for every requested length, such a set contains a progression with positive common difference.
>
> The selected theorem is the reciprocal-sum consequence. The paper's quantitative upper bound for the largest progression-free subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is outside this statement.

Comparator source `ErdosReciprocal.lean` (626 bytes, sha256 `0df84b7d562a557f7bfc540d4c117f66c5352c564bf8e3b5f5f6d0d504ffbc3f`), verbatim:

```lean
import Mathlib

namespace OAI

namespace Erdos3

def HasAP (A : Set ℕ) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ a d : ℕ, 0 < d ∧ ∀ i < k, a + i * d ∈ A

end Erdos3

open scoped BigOperators

namespace Erdos3

noncomputable def reciprocalTerm (A : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℝ := by
  classical
  exact if n ∈ A then (n : ℝ)⁻¹ else 0

end Erdos3

namespace Erdos3

def ReciprocalProgressionTheorem : Prop :=
  ∀ A : Set ℕ, ¬ Summable (reciprocalTerm A) → ∀ k : ℕ, HasAP A k

end Erdos3

namespace Erdos3

theorem manuscriptReciprocalProgressionTheorem : ReciprocalProgressionTheorem := by
  sorry

end Erdos3

end OAI
```

<a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


We prove Erdős's conjecture that every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. More quantitatively, for every fixed <i>k</i> ≥ 3, we show

$`\displaystyle r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr)`$

with $`C_k,c_k,\varepsilon_k\gt 0`$, where $`r_k(N)`$ is the largest size of a subset of $`\{1,\ldots,N\}`$ with no nonconstant <i>k</i>-term arithmetic progression.

<a id="ap:introduction"></a>
### Introduction

Erdős asked whether every set $A$ of positive integers for which $\sum_{a\in A}1/a$ diverges contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[Erdos1974](#ref-Erdos1974), Problem 4.33.6]. We prove a quantitative density bound that implies this assertion. For integers $k\ge3$ and $N\ge1$, let $r_k(N)$ be the largest cardinality of a subset of $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing no nonconstant $k$-term arithmetic progression $a,a+d,\ldots,a+(k-1)d$, with $d>0$. All logarithms are natural.

<a id="stmt-ap-main"></a>
<div id="ap:main" class="theorem">

<a id="ap:density-bound"></a>
<a id="ap:threshold"></a>
**Theorem 1**. *For each fixed integer $k\ge3$ there are constants $C_k,c_k,\varepsilon_k>0$ such that, for every $N\ge2$, $$\label{ap:density-bound}
 r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr).$$ Equivalently, there is $A_k\ge1$ such that an $\alpha$-dense subset of $[N]$ contains a nonconstant $k$-term progression whenever $$\label{ap:threshold}
 \log N\ge A_k\bigl(2+\log(1/\alpha)\bigr)^{A_k},
 \qquad 0<\alpha\le1.$$*

</div>

The constants may depend on the fixed length $k$; the exponent is not optimized. The reciprocal-sum consequence follows immediately from summing the density bound over dyadic intervals.

<a id="stmt-ap-reciprocal"></a>
<div id="ap:reciprocal" class="corollary">

**Corollary 2** (Divergent reciprocal sums). *Every set $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{a\in A}a^{-1}=\infty$ contains nonconstant arithmetic progressions of every finite length.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ap-reciprocal"><summary>Proof of stmt-ap-reciprocal</summary>

*Proof.* Fix $k\ge3$, and suppose that $A$ contains no nonconstant $k$-term progression. For $m\ge0$, translation identifies $[2^m,2^{m+1})\cap\mathbb Z$ with an interval of length $2^m$. Thus $|A\cap[2^m,2^{m+1})|\le r_k(2^m)$. Theorem <a href="#ap:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:main">1</a> implies, for $m\ge1$, $$\sum_{a\in A\cap[2^m,2^{m+1})}\frac1a
 \le 2^{-m}r_k(2^m)
 \le C_k\exp\bigl(-c_k(m\log2)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr).$$ For every $d,\varepsilon>0$, the sequence $e^{-dm^\varepsilon}$ is summable: since $m^\varepsilon/\log m\to\infty$, its terms are at most $m^{-2}$ for all sufficiently large $m$. The $m=0$ interval contributes at most one. The reciprocal sum of $A$ is therefore finite, a contradiction. Divergence also implies that $A$ is infinite, which supplies lengths one and two. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-3"></a>
#### Density thresholds and summability

The threshold in <a href="#ap:threshold" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ap:threshold">[ap:threshold]</a> is quasipolynomial in $1/\alpha$: the logarithm of a sufficient interval length is a fixed power of $2+\log(1/\alpha)$. The inversion between the two forms of Theorem <a href="#ap:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:main">1</a>, including the endpoints, is proved in Section <a href="#ap:iteration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:iteration">10</a>.

The infinite-set consequence depends on more than a density tending to zero. Divergence of a reciprocal sum allows zero-density sets, and the qualitative estimate $r_k(N)=o(N)$ does not by itself settle Erdős’s question. The proof of Corollary <a href="#ap:reciprocal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:reciprocal">2</a> uses the stronger condition $$\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{r_k(2^m)}{2^m}<\infty.$$ Our bound also gives a stronger divergence criterion: for every fixed $B\ge0$, a set $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ satisfying $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac{(\log(2+a))^B}{a}=\infty$$ contains progressions of every finite length. Section <a href="#ap:weighted" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:weighted">11</a> proves this criterion, uniform harmonic bounds and tails, and estimates for larger weights whose parameters depend on $k$. It also recovers the theorem of Green and Tao that every subset of the primes of positive relative upper density contains infinitely many progressions of every finite length <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[GreenTaoPrimes2008](#ref-GreenTaoPrimes2008), Theorem 1.2].

<a id="pm-h-4"></a>
#### Prior density bounds

Van der Waerden’s theorem concerns a partition: every finite coloring of the positive integers has a monochromatic arithmetic progression of each finite length <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[vanDerWaerden1927](#ref-vanDerWaerden1927)]. The density problem asks for a condition on a prescribed set. Erdős and Turán began the study of the corresponding extremal functions in 1936 and explicitly conjectured that $r_3(N)=o(N)$ <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[ErdosTuran1936](#ref-ErdosTuran1936)]. The all-length positive-density conjecture appears explicitly in Erdős’s later account <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[Erdos1961](#ref-Erdos1961), Section I.19]. Roth proved the three-term case by Fourier-analytic methods <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[Roth1953](#ref-Roth1953)]; Szemerédi proved the four-term case in 1969 and the general theorem in 1975 . Furstenberg’s subsequent proof recast the assertion as multiple recurrence in a measure-preserving system <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[Furstenberg1977](#ref-Furstenberg1977)]. The reciprocal-sum conjecture extends this density problem to sparser sets, including the primes <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[Erdos1974](#ref-Erdos1974), Problem 4.33.6].

For three terms, successive quantitative advances sharpened Roth’s density-increment method: a shortage of progressions forces a density increase on a smaller structured set. Roth obtained $r_3(N)\ll N/\log\log N$. Heath-Brown and Szemerédi replaced the double logarithm by a positive power of $\log N$ <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[HeathBrown1987](#ref-HeathBrown1987), [Szemeredi1990](#ref-Szemeredi1990)], and Bourgain developed density increments on regular Bohr sets <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[Bourgain1999](#ref-Bourgain1999), [Bourgain2008](#ref-Bourgain2008)]. Sanders reached $r_3(N)\ll N/(\log N)^{1-o(1)}$, and Bloom improved the remaining logarithmic factors <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[Sanders2011](#ref-Sanders2011), [Bloom2016](#ref-Bloom2016)]. Bloom and Sisask gave an almost-periodicity approach to this near-logarithmic range <a id="pm-cite-12"></a>[[BloomSisask2019](#ref-BloomSisask2019)]. Their later bound $r_3(N)\ll N/(\log N)^{1+c}$, for an absolute $c>0$, crossed the dyadic summability threshold and established the three-term reciprocal-sum conjecture <a id="pm-cite-13"></a>[[BloomSisask2020](#ref-BloomSisask2020)].

Kelley and Meka obtained the stronger bound $$r_3(N)\ll N\exp\bigl(-c(\log N)^{1/12}\bigr)$$ by combining positivity, dependent-random-choice sifting and almost-periodicity to control the loss in a density increment <a id="pm-cite-14"></a>[[KelleyMeka2023](#ref-KelleyMeka2023)]. Bloom and Sisask simplified the argument and then improved the exponent to $1/9$ <a id="pm-cite-15"></a>[[BloomSisaskKelleyMeka](#ref-BloomSisaskKelleyMeka), [BloomSisaskImprovement2023](#ref-BloomSisaskImprovement2023)]. Raghavan subsequently obtained $r_3(N)\le N\exp\bigl(-(\log N)^{1/6-o(1)}\bigr)$ <a id="pm-cite-16"></a>[[Raghavan2026](#ref-Raghavan2026), Theorem 1.4]. These refinements concern three terms. On the lower-bound side, Behrend’s construction already gives $r_3(N)\ge N\exp(-C\sqrt{\log N})$, so a fixed power saving in $N$ is impossible even in this case <a id="pm-cite-17"></a>[[Behrend1946](#ref-Behrend1946)].

Gowers’s approach to longer progressions detects higher-order structure. He introduced the uniformity norms that control progression counts and extended density increments beyond linear Fourier analysis <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[Gowers1998](#ref-Gowers1998), [Gowers2001](#ref-Gowers2001)]. His general theorem gives $r_k(N)\ll_k N/(\log\log N)^{c_k}$ for every fixed $k$, with $c_k>0$. Green and Tao obtained $r_4(N)\ll N/(\log N)^c$ <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[GreenTao2017](#ref-GreenTao2017)]. Leng, Sah and Sawhney first treated five terms and then proved, for every fixed $k\ge5$, $$r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp\bigl(-(\log\log N)^{c_k}\bigr),
 \qquad 0<c_k<1$$ <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[LengSahSawhneyFive](#ref-LengSahSawhneyFive), [LSSSzemeredi2024](#ref-LSSSzemeredi2024)]. Their general argument combines a quasipolynomial inverse theorem with density increments. The inverse theorem controls the structured correlation obtained from a large uniformity norm; the cost of localizing and iterating that correlation remains a separate issue. The resulting saving in $\log\log N$ does not give the dyadic summability above.

Theorem <a href="#ap:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:main">1</a> gives a stretched-exponential saving in $\log N$ for every fixed length. Its contribution to Erdős’s conjecture is this all-length, summable bound; no improvement of the three-term exponent is claimed. We next explain the quantitative constraint on the density-increment regions that allows the argument to be iterated at this scale.

<a id="pm-h-5"></a>
#### Preserving structure through density increments

A fixed multiplicative density gain can be applied only $O_k(1+\log(1/\alpha))$ times before the density exceeds one. To obtain Theorem <a href="#ap:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:main">1</a>, the total logarithmic loss of interval length over these increments must be polynomial in $2+\log(1/\alpha)$. We therefore need to control both the number of coordinates describing each new region and the precision of the constraints inherited from previous regions.

The regions are triangular polynomial cells. A spatial integer variable $u$ determines integer blocks $b_1,\ldots,b_D$ successively through constraints of the form $$\|b_h-C_h(u,b_1,\ldots,b_{h-1})-l_h\|_\infty\le w_h,
 \qquad 1\le h\le D,\qquad 0<w_h\le1/32.$$ Here $D$ depends only on $k$, each $l_h$ is a fixed center, and $C_h$ is a polynomial. The spatial variable has weight one, the block $b_h$ has weight $h$, and $C_h$ has weighted degree at most $h$. The narrow widths make each integer block unique when it exists. Keeping these integer blocks, and substituting them exactly into all later polynomials, preserves the equations defining the old region when a new constraint is added. No bound on the coefficients of the $C_h$ is imposed.

Write $Q_h=\log(2/w_h)$ for the precision at weight $h$. The main increment theorem bounds the *additional* precision at weight $h$ by a polynomial in the dimension data, the logarithmic density parameter, and the precisions at strictly higher weights. In particular, this bound does not use the current $Q_h$ or the lower precisions. The dimensions obey an analogous descending recurrence. Since the number $D$ of weights is fixed, descending induction bounds all dimensions and precisions by polynomials through the required number of increments. Section <a href="#ap:setup" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:setup">2</a> states these recurrences precisely; Section <a href="#ap:iteration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:iteration">10</a> proves that the construction satisfies them.

Two different arguments supply these bounds. The first produces an *absolute increment* for a $[0,1]$-valued function on an integer box with sufficiently long sides. The function must have positive mean and contain no nonconstant $k$-term progression in its support. The increment adds only a number of determining coordinates polynomial in the logarithmic inverse mean, independently of the dimension of that box. The second returns such an increment from a sampled box to the original cell, preserving the old determining equations and the descending dependence of their width losses. An absolute increment with uncontrolled dependence on the old widths would not suffice for this second task.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
###### The absolute increment.

The higher-order inverse theorem converts a large uniformity norm into correlation with a nilsequence, a Lipschitz function evaluated along a polynomial orbit on a compact nilmanifold. This description of structured correlations has both ergodic and additive-combinatorial origins. Host and Kra developed seminorms and nilsystem characteristic factors, Ziegler proved the universal-factor theorem, and Bergelson, Host and Kra isolated nilsequences in multiple correlations <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[HostKra2005](#ref-HostKra2005), [Ziegler2007](#ref-Ziegler2007), [BergelsonHostKra2005](#ref-BergelsonHostKra2005)]. Green and Tao obtained locally quadratic structure for the $U^3$ norm <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[GreenTaoU32008](#ref-GreenTaoU32008)]; Green, Tao and Ziegler then proved the all-degree interval inverse theorem <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[GreenTaoZiegler2012](#ref-GreenTaoZiegler2012)]. Manners gave explicit quantitative inverse bounds on prime cyclic groups <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[Manners2018](#ref-Manners2018)]. The stronger quasipolynomial bounds of Leng, Sah and Sawhney are the interval input used here <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[LSSInverse2024](#ref-LSSInverse2024), Theorem 1.2]; the appendices prove the box and product-cyclic reductions needed in the argument.

To pass from structured tests to positive progression counting, we prove a shift-comparison theorem: lowering the testing degree permits multiplication by a translated nonnegative function outside a small exceptional set of shifts. Its degree-one argument adapts Kelley–Meka unbalancing and sifting, as developed on Bohr sets by Bloom and Sisask <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[KelleyMeka2023](#ref-KelleyMeka2023), [BloomSisaskKelleyMeka](#ref-BloomSisaskKelleyMeka)]. The almost-periodicity input is Schoen–Sisask’s Theorem 5.4 . It combines the probabilistic method of Croot and Sisask with Sanders’s local control of large spectra <a id="pm-cite-27"></a>[[CrootSisask2010](#ref-CrootSisask2010), [SandersSumsets2008](#ref-SandersSumsets2008)]; see also Sanders’s Bogolyubov–Ruzsa theorem <a id="pm-cite-28"></a>[[SandersBogolyubov2012](#ref-SandersBogolyubov2012)]. The Schoen–Sisask radius bound retains the incoming radius as a multiplicative factor, which is essential for the shift comparison.

Higher-degree comparison requires control of polynomial orbits. Leibman established a qualitative distribution theorem <a id="pm-cite-29"></a>[[Leibman2005](#ref-Leibman2005)]. Green and Tao made this theory quantitative and factored polynomial orbits into smooth, equidistributed and rational components <a id="pm-cite-30"></a>[[GreenTaoOrbits2012](#ref-GreenTaoOrbits2012)]. Leng’s efficient estimates reduce the nilpotency step rather than repeatedly reducing the dimension <a id="pm-cite-31"></a>[[LengEquidistribution2023](#ref-LengEquidistribution2023)]. We use this mechanism, together with the inverse theorem, to remove top-degree frequencies in the comparison argument. The appendices prove the required forms with explicit dependence on all growing dimensions and parameter counts.

The comparison and counting arguments first give the absolute rule in a fixed dimension. A relative lifting theorem extends it with only an additive number of new determining coordinates. Applied with the constant old region, this yields the dimension-independent fresh-coordinate bound in Lemma <a href="#ap:absolute" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:absolute">4</a>. This foundational lifting argument supplies the absolute rule; preservation of the old width budgets requires the separate return argument.

<a id="pm-h-7"></a>
###### Returning to the original cell.

A density increment found on a sampled parameter box must be expressed again in the original variables. The cell can have very small mass, and an error in one of its determining integers would enter every later polynomial that uses that integer. The return therefore keeps the old equations exact.

For tests of degree below the current layer weight, we use a cube version of Conlon–Fox–Zhao densification to replace sparse factors by bounded ones before applying inverse theory <a id="pm-cite-32"></a>[[ConlonFoxZhao2015](#ref-ConlonFoxZhao2015)]. The comparison proved here has bounds independent of that layer’s chart mass. At layers where the testing degree is at least the layer weight, polynomial families retain the old equations through an exact projection while allowing the newly added region to have higher degree. Preparation, ascent and extraction then control the relative loss of each width by structural data and higher-weight precision budgets. The general route from inverse theory to density increments is classical <a id="pm-cite-33"></a>[[GreenTaoDensity2010](#ref-GreenTaoDensity2010)]; retaining this dependence through the return is the quantitative issue addressed here.

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
#### Coloring thresholds

Let $W_r(k)$ be the least integer $N$ such that every coloring of $[N]$ with $r$ colors contains a monochromatic nonconstant $k$-term arithmetic progression. A largest color class has density at least $1/r$, so Theorem <a href="#ap:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:main">1</a> gives <a id="ap:coloring"></a>$$\label{ap:coloring}
 W_r(k)\le
 \left\lceil\exp\bigl(A_k(2+\log r)^{A_k}\bigr)\right\rceil
 \qquad(r\ge1),$$ after increasing $A_k$. Thus, for fixed $k$, the sufficient length is quasipolynomial in the number of colors. The companion paper <a id="pm-cite-34"></a>[[OpenAIVanDerWaerden2026](#ref-OpenAIVanDerWaerden2026), Theorem 7.2] gives the complementary lower bound $W_r(k)>\exp((\log r)^2/(64\log2))$ for all integers $r\ge256$ and $k\ge3$. Together these estimates show that for each fixed $k\ge3$, growth in the number of colors is superpolynomial but at most quasipolynomial. The upper constant and exponent may depend on $k$.

<a id="pm-h-9"></a>
#### How to read the proof

Section <a href="#ap:setup" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:setup">2</a> defines the cells and precision budgets, states the triangular increment theorem, and explains the dimension-independent absolute rule. Figure <a href="#ap:proof-route" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:proof-route">3</a> gives the main route, and Table <a href="#ap:interface-table" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:interface-table">1</a> identifies the analytic statements and their full proofs. Section <a href="#ap:paths" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:paths">3</a> constructs the constrained path law and states its sampling guarantees. Section <a href="#ap:preparation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:preparation">4</a> prepares the cell by rank cuts, and Section <a href="#ap:relative-detection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:relative-detection">5</a> proves the detection bound independent of the current width. Section <a href="#ap:scalar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:scalar">6</a> transfers the certificate to terminal boxes and obtains an absolute increment. Section <a href="#ap:ascent" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:ascent">7</a> sets up its return, develops the comparison estimates, and handles the passive layers. Section <a href="#ap:active" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:active">8</a> treats the active layers. Section <a href="#ap:extraction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:extraction">9</a> extracts the next cell, and Section <a href="#ap:iteration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:iteration">10</a> closes the recurrences and proves Theorem <a href="#ap:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:main">1</a>. Section <a href="#ap:weighted" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:weighted">11</a> establishes the weighted consequences.

The appendices contain the rational and symbol calculus, shift comparison, progression counting, constrained sampling, cube comparison and relative lifting arguments. The two principal external analytic inputs to the increment proof are the interval inverse theorem of Leng, Sah and Sawhney and the radius-sensitive almost-periodicity theorem of Schoen and Sisask <a id="pm-cite-35"></a>[[LSSInverse2024](#ref-LSSInverse2024), [SchoenSisask2016](#ref-SchoenSisask2016)]. Their precise hypotheses are stated at the points of application.

<a id="ap:setup"></a>
### Polynomial cells and the increment theorem

Fix $k\ge3$ and put $s=k-2$. We seek density increments on regions that retain every polynomial constraint introduced by an earlier increment. The regions will be triangular polynomial cells. Their integer coordinates are determined successively, and their residual widths are indexed by weight. The central estimate will bound the relative width loss at each weight using only higher-weight widths.

Every degree and descent depth below is fixed in terms of $s$; dimensions may grow. A degree bound may be replaced by any fixed larger one. We work on rectangular integer boxes, with uniform probability averages and max norms, allowing dimension factors in norm comparisons. A *slice* is an integer-affinely reindexed residue subbox. Different coordinate strides are permitted. Its logarithmic cost includes their logarithms and the logarithms of inverse relative side lengths. Sufficient lower bounds on the original sides absorb all endpoint rounding errors. A function is *progression-free* when its support contains no nonconstant integer-vector $k$-term progression.

<a id="pm-h-11"></a>
#### Precision conventions

Write $\mathcal P(P)=(2+P)^C$ and $\mathcal B(P)=\exp((2+P)^C)$, with $C$ depending only on the fixed degrees and allowed to increase. A quantity has polynomial *logarithmic* cost when its size and, when needed, inverse size are at most $\mathcal B(P)$. Dimensions, numbers of structural variables, and polynomial degrees are not measured logarithmically. Only a bounded number of successive polynomial changes of budget is implicit; a polynomial number of multiplicative factors is permitted because their logarithmic costs add. The height of rational data bounds both numerators and positive denominators; a denominator bound alone leaves numerators unrestricted. Multiplying a density threshold by a fixed positive constant changes its logarithmic budget by only a fixed additive amount. We absorb such changes in the displayed polynomial bounds, including the fresh rank bound $d_0$, whenever a discounted threshold is used.

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
#### Cells and certificates

Choose a fixed $D\ge s$, whose existence is verified by the weight argument in Section <a href="#ap:extraction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:extraction">9</a>. Give the spatial variable $u$ weight one and integer blocks $b_h\in\mathbb Z^{d_h}$ weight $h$, for $1\le h\le D$. The weighted degree of a monomial is the sum of its variable weights, counted with multiplicity. A triangular cell is specified by polynomials $$C_h(u,b_{<h})\in\mathbb R^{d_h},\qquad \deg_{\rm wt}C_h\le h,$$ bounded centers $l_h$, and widths $0<w_h\le1/32$. There is no bound on the coefficients of $C_h$. Integer translations keep the centers bounded without changing this convention. Zero-dimensional blocks are allowed. Put $$Q_h=\log(2/w_h).$$ Thus $Q_h$ measures the logarithmic precision of the residual at weight $h$.

<a id="ap:certificate"></a>
For a small $\gamma>0$, let $B^-$ and $B^+$ be the indicators that there is an integer tuple satisfying respectively <a id="ap:cell-boxes"></a>$$\label{ap:cell-boxes}
 \|b_h-C_h(u,b_{<h})-l_h\|_\infty\le w_h,
 \qquad
 \|b_h-C_h(u,b_{<h})-l_h\|_\infty\le(1+\gamma)w_h
 \quad(1\le h\le D).$$ Triangularity and the narrow widths imply uniqueness of the tuple, also on slightly padded boxes. Boundary conventions may be chosen consistently and do not require any regularity of the point distribution. A *density certificate* is $$\label{ap:certificate}
                 \mathbb EfB^- > a\mathbb EB^+,
 \qquad 0\le f\le1,$$ where $f$ is progression-free. Its excess is not assumed to have a quantitative lower bound.

We may replace the two indicators temporarily by product smooth cutoffs: the small cutoff is below the strict indicator, and the large cutoff is one on the enlarged box and supported slightly outside it. Their plateaus and transitions are proportional to the width and gap. When translating small boxes, the ratio of enlarged to strict coverage volumes is $(1+O(\gamma))^{O(\sum_h d_h)}$. We choose $\gamma$ from dimension forecasts, independently of all widths, and pay this ratio by a small multiplicative discount of the target. Thus no hidden boundary regularity assertion is needed.

<a id="pm-h-13"></a>
#### The triangular increment

The new cell will retain the old determining coordinates and may add two kinds of integer coordinates. Fresh *absolute slots* come from the analytic increment. Preparation may also copy a higher-weight block into a lower-weight block. The following theorem controls both additions and the loss of residual width.

<a id="stmt-ap-increment"></a>
<div id="ap:increment" class="theorem">

**Theorem 3** (Triangular increment). *There are fixed $D=D_k$, $\eta=\eta_k>0$, and polynomials with degrees depending only on $k$ having the following property. Suppose $p\ge2$, $a\ge e^{-p}$, and a progression-free input on a positive-dimensional integer box has a certificate <a href="#ap:certificate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ap:certificate">[ap:certificate]</a>, with width logs $Q_h=\log(2/w_h)$. If every root side is sufficiently large with logarithmic cutoff polynomial in $p$, the dimension data, and all $Q_h$, then either the hypotheses are impossible or a root slice carries a new certificate at threshold $(1+\eta)a$.*

<a id="ap:width-rule"></a>
*The new cell retains the determining data through exact integer reparametrizations and adds at most $d_0=(2+p)^{C_k}$ fresh absolute slots together with downward preparation copies. Its dimensions $d'_i$ and width logs $Q'_i$ satisfy <a id="ap:dimension-rule"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 d'_i-d_i
   &\le d_0+P_i(p,d_{i+1},\ldots,d_D),\label{ap:dimension-rule}\\
 Q'_i-Q_i
   &\le P'_i(p,\text{all dimension forecasts},Q_{i+1},\ldots,Q_D).
   \label{ap:width-rule}
\end{aligned}$$ The root slice cost has polynomial logarithmic bound in all the same data, now including every $Q_i$. Polynomial exponents and the fixed gain are independent of the number of increments. Gap and discount choices can be made in advance from the dimension and cut-count forecasts.*

</div>

The main point is the absence of $Q_i,Q_{<i}$ from the right-hand side of <a href="#ap:width-rule" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ap:width-rule">[ap:width-rule]</a>. For the interval application, reserve $T=O_k(p)$ increments, starting with no slots and fixed width data. The dimension recurrence first bounds the top block, then each lower block. Proposition <a href="#ap:iteration:dimensions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:iteration:dimensions">39</a> verifies this recurrence for the actual preparation copies and bounds all within-round structural counts. It supplies one polynomial forecast $d_*(p)$ for the entire run, before any numerical precision is chosen.

With that forecast fixed, choose nondecreasing polynomials $R_i$ dominating the width losses in <a href="#ap:width-rule" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ap:width-rule">[ap:width-rule]</a>. Define $$V_D=Q_D(0)+T R_D(p,d_*),\qquad
 V_i=Q_i(0)+T R_i(p,d_*,V_{i+1},\ldots,V_D)
 \quad(i=D-1,\ldots,1).$$ Descending induction gives $Q_i(t)\le V_i$ for all $t\le T$. Since $D$ is fixed, every $V_i$ is polynomial in $p$. The logarithmic root-side requirements and the sum of all logarithmic slice costs are therefore polynomial as well. Meanwhile the threshold rises by a fixed factor at every increment and, after $O_k(p)$ steps, exceeds one. A certificate at threshold at least one is impossible because $fB^-\le B^+$ pointwise. Section <a href="#ap:iteration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:iteration">10</a> makes this deduction precise and proves the required dimension and width recurrences.

It remains to construct the increment with these particular dependencies. A bound polynomial in all current width logs would not suffice: repeated substitution could raise the polynomial degree at every round.

<a id="ap:analytic-objects"></a>
#### Polynomial patches

The analytic increment produces a smooth test rather than a cell indicator. These tests are polynomial patches; their integer slots will supply the new absolute coordinates. Give integer slots $b_1,\ldots,b_d$ nondecreasing weights $1\le\omega_i\le q$, and give each spatial parameter weight one. A degree-$q$ *patch* is <a id="ap:patch-definition"></a>$$\label{ap:patch-definition}
 B(u)=\sum_{b\in\mathbb Z^d}\Phi(S_u(b)),\qquad
 S_u(b)_i=b_i-A_i(u,b_1,\ldots,b_{i-1}),$$ where $\deg_{\rm wt}A_i\le\omega_i$ and $\Phi:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]$ is Lipschitz and supported in $[-1/4,1/4]^d$. Its *rank* is the number $d$ of integer slots. The number of parameters, $d$, and $\log(2+\mathop{\mathrm{Lip}}\Phi)$ enter its logarithmic complexity; the coefficients of the $A_i$ do not. Rank zero includes the constant patch $1$. Successively determining the integer slots shows that at most one summand is nonzero, so $0\le B\le1$. Figure <a href="#fig:patch-coordinates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="fig:patch-coordinates">1</a> illustrates the distinction between integer determining slots and small real residuals. For a nonnegative test $B$, its *score at target $a$* is $\mathbb E(f-a)B$. Positivity means that the mean of $f$ under the probability weight $B/\mathbb EB$ exceeds $a$; a quantitative lower bound on the score also controls the available mass.

<figure id="fig:patch-coordinates">

<figcaption>A degree-two patch of rank two, with slot weights $1, 2$, at $u = 1$. Here $A_{1}(u) = u$, $A_{2}(u,b_{1}) = (u^{2}+ub_{1})/2$, and $S_{1}(b_{1},b_{2}) = (b_{1}−1,b_{2}−(1+b_{1})/2)$. The shaded parallelogram is the inverse image of $[−1/4,1/4]^{2}$, the permitted support of the kernel. Only the integer pair $(1,1)$ lies in it. For a general patch, at most one integer tuple satisfies the support constraints, by successive determination of the slots.</figcaption>
</figure>

<a id="pm-h-15"></a>
#### The absolute starting rule

Positive progression counting first gives an increment on boxes of a fixed dimension. Relative lifting transfers that rule to arbitrary dimension while keeping the number of new slots separate from the other complexity costs. The following form is used at the terminal boxes of the cell argument.

<a id="stmt-ap-absolute"></a>
<div id="ap:absolute" class="lemma">

**Lemma 4** (Dimension-independent fresh rank). *There are $\xi>0$ and $C=C_k$ with the following property. Let $p\ge2$, and let $f$ be a progression-free $[0,1]$-valued function of mean at least $a\ge e^{-p}$ on a box of positive dimension $n$. Suppose every side is sufficiently large, with a sufficient logarithmic cutoff polynomial in $2+p+n$. Then, unless the hypotheses are impossible, $f$ admits a degree-$s$ polynomial patch on a slice with positive score at target $(1+\xi)a$. The number of slots is at most $d_0=(2+p)^C$, independent of $n$. The logarithms of inverse score, Lipschitz norm, slice cost, and sufficient side cutoff are polynomial in $2+p+n$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ap-absolute"><summary>Proof of stmt-ap-absolute</summary>

*Proof.* Fix the base dimension $n_0(s)$ and prime-side comparability constant in Proposition <a href="#counting:relative-target" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="counting:relative-target">76</a>. Proposition <a href="#counting:absolute" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="counting:absolute">72</a>, Lemma <a href="#counting:conversion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="counting:conversion">74</a>, and Theorem <a href="#shift:required" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:required">58</a> give an absolute rule on these fixed-dimensional boxes, with gain $1+\xi_0$ and rank $(2+p)^{C_k}$. The side cutoff absorbs all three requirements; the prime sides can be odd.

Choose a small fixed $c>0$. At any actual mean $\alpha\ge(1-c)a$, the absolute rule has logarithmic budget $O(1+p)$ and gives positive score at the universal smaller target $\Lambda=(1+\xi_0)(1-c)a$. If $\Lambda\ge1$, its nonnegative test gives an impossibility rule instead. In the relative theorem use the constant old test $1$, of rank zero, at threshold $(1-c)a$. Its old score is at least $ca$. Enlarge the resource parameter to a polynomial in $p+n$ to cover the dimension, absolute cutoff, and $\log(1/(ca))$. Theorem <a href="#lifting:relative-theorem" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lifting:relative-theorem">124</a> proves Proposition <a href="#counting:relative-target" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="counting:relative-target">76</a>, including its separate impossibility clause. Its rank conclusion is $d+d_0$, so the enlarged resource parameter does not enlarge the fresh rank $d_0$. Choose its fixed target discount $\epsilon_0$ and then $c$ so that $(1-\epsilon_0)(1+\xi_0)(1-c)>1+\xi$ for a fixed $\xi>0$. This gives the claimed rule and all its quantitative bounds. ◻

</details>

<a id="ap:scalar-conventions"></a>
#### Scalar rank and scale conventions

Preparation tests the homogeneous parts of the determining polynomials. For a box with side lengths $H=(H_1,\ldots,H_n)$, write $H^\nu=\prod_iH_i^{\nu_i}$. A homogeneous scalar or vector polynomial is *slow* at budget $p$ if its coefficient of $u^\nu$ has magnitude at most $\mathcal B(p)H^{-\nu}$. It is *rational* if its coefficients have a common denominator at most $\mathcal B(p)$, with no numerator bound. The homogeneous part at the assigned degree or weight is called its *symbol*. A polynomial is *fully slow* when the same coefficient bounds hold at every degree, including the constant coefficient, after the box has been translated to the origin. Thus real estimates use normalized variables, while denominator estimates use the raw integer variables. Group-valued symbols are introduced with the ascent representation in Section <a href="#ap:ascent" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:ascent">7</a>.

<a id="ap:rank-conventions"></a>
##### Formal rank

Suppose a degree-$j$ polynomial $C_j$ takes values in a rational space $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_j}$ on a box of sides $H$. It has rank at least $R$ at this scale if every integer row $\lambda\in\mathbb Z^{d_j}$ with $\|\lambda\|\le R$ and $\lambda|_{W_j}\ne0$ has the following property: the degree-$j$ homogeneous part of $\lambda C_j$ cannot be written as a polynomial whose coefficient of $u^\nu$ is bounded by $R/H^\nu$ plus a rational polynomial with common denominator at most $R$. For a system, this condition is imposed at every layer. This is the rank condition of Definition <a href="#sampling:rank" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:rank">85</a>; it is different from the slot count called the rank of a patch.

<a id="pm-h-18"></a>
#### Descending precision budgets

<a id="stmt-ap-budgets"></a>
<div id="ap:budgets" class="definition">

**Definition 5** (Descending budgets). At layer $j$, the *warm data* consist of $p$, forecasts for all dimensions and structural variable counts, gap parameters depending only on these data, and the widths and numerical budgets already chosen at layers strictly above $j$. A warm logarithmic bound is polynomial in these data and does not use any $Q_i$ with $i\le j$.

The *cold preliminary data* may additionally use the current width log $Q_j$, including its forecast preparation losses, but not the eventual rank threshold, long path scale, height of the prepared value space, or parent-side cutoff at layer $j$. The *late data* are the perturbation, range, rank, and side choices made after all preliminary modeling and algebraic requirements at that layer. Their logarithms are polynomial in the cold preliminary budget.

</div>

The descending choice order is opposite to the order in which paths are sampled through the layers. Auxiliary models may have cold complexity. Their eventual return to the original variables must nevertheless have a warm *relative width loss*; the extraction argument preserves the defining polynomial maps exactly. Figure <a href="#ap:budget-figure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:budget-figure">2</a> displays the permitted dependence.

</figure>

<a id="pm-h-19"></a>
#### From a cell to the next certificate

Preparation removes low-rank relations while preserving the certificate (Proposition <a href="#ap:major:preparation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:major:preparation">10</a>). Constrained paths then carry it to terminal boxes (Proposition <a href="#ap:scalar:forward" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:scalar:forward">21</a>), where Lemma <a href="#ap:absolute" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:absolute">4</a> supplies a quantitative score. The passive and active return arguments carry that score back through the layers (Proposition <a href="#ap:passive:replacement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:passive:replacement">29</a> and Theorem <a href="#ap:active:replacement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:active:replacement">32</a>). Extraction turns the returned score into a triangular cell (Proposition <a href="#ap:macro:extraction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:macro:extraction">34</a>). Finally, Section <a href="#ap:iteration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:iteration">10</a> verifies the dimension and width bounds and iterates the increment.

<figcaption>The main proof route. Preparation and extraction preserve the triangular dependence of the width losses; the absolute increment controls the number of fresh determining coordinates.</figcaption>
</figure>

During preparation the polynomial $C_j$ takes values exactly in a rational subspace $W_j\subseteq E_j=\mathbb R^{d_j}$, initially the full space. The rank test defined above and in Definition <a href="#sampling:rank" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:rank">85</a> requires that no integer row of norm at most $R_j$, nonzero on $W_j$, has a degree-$j$ symbol that is slow plus rational at that threshold. The test is made on the current path box at a history that has survived the earlier tests. The histories arriving at each layer carry the subprobability law of Section <a href="#ap:path:stopped-tree" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:path:stopped-tree">3.5</a>; stopping removes mass without renormalizing the survivors. Its failure probability may charge $Q_{\ge j}$ but not lower widths. There is no single root equidistribution test at the finest precision of all layers.

At a successful layer use a Haar center in $W_j/(W_j\cap\mathbb Z^{d_j})$, conditioned to the feasible range specified in Section <a href="#ap:path:stopped-tree" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:path:stopped-tree">3.5</a>. The lift has exact identity $$C_j-c=y+\beta,$$ where $y\in\mathbb R^{d_j}$ is the small real residual and $\beta\in\mathbb Z^{d_j}$ is the integer lift. The raw determining slot is $b_j=\beta+b_{j,0}$ for a constant integer vector. This convention matters: every later old polynomial uses the actual integer slot, not an approximation to its value. Structural numbers of path columns are fixed polynomials of the input dimensions before any numerical precision is chosen. Consequently all ambient dimensions along a branch are polynomial in the current dimension forecasts. Sides are selected to support the next layer and finally Lemma <a href="#ap:absolute" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:absolute">4</a>.

The return processes layers from $D$ down to $1$. Layers $j>s$ are passive: the new patch does not acquire their integer arguments. At the final $s$ active layers its weights may increase by fixed factors, while the old determining equations and their weights stay exact. This distinction is why a fixed $D$ can be chosen before the iteration, even though the number of slots grows.

The input certificate and the returned score carry different information. Preparation needs only the strict inequality in the input certificate: its selections do not charge the inverse of that inequality’s excess. Proposition <a href="#ap:scalar:forward" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:scalar:forward">21</a> then gives terminal means near the current threshold on a quantitatively large set of paths. Lemma <a href="#ap:absolute" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:absolute">4</a> supplies the quantitative score needed for ascent. Thus all subsequent approximation accuracies can be chosen from the recorded budgets, independently of the original excess.

The analytic proofs are grouped separately. Table <a href="#ap:interface-table" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:interface-table">1</a>, at the entrance to that part, locates each input statement and its proof.

<a id="ap:paths"></a>
### Constrained paths and their detection estimates

At one layer of a triangular cell, we seek many integer-affine maps $\psi(t)=x+Vt$ along which the current polynomial has a small polynomial residual and an exact integer-polynomial lift. The affine maps preserve arithmetic progressions; the polynomial identity will preserve the determining equations when a new patch is returned to the parent. We construct their probability law in this section.

There are two comparison estimates to prove for that law. With the center fixed, tests chosen separately on the sampled boxes must be detectable on the parent. After averaging the center, the one-site distribution must approximate the parent distribution. Below the current degree, the first comparison must be measured relative to the small chart: charging its reciprocal mass to the output complexity would charge the current width to its own relative loss.

The coefficient density will be a product law on an abstract coefficient torus. The actual ensemble is the integer spatial law weighted by that density. These are different probability spaces. The construction below defines both; high rank will supply the comparison between them. The general estimates for coefficient modes and polynomial images are proved in Appendices <a href="#sampling:constrained-section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:constrained-section">17</a> and <a href="#cube:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cube:section">18</a>.

Throughout this section, $j$ is the current layer, $d=d_j$, $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ is rational, and $$U=\prod_{a=1}^n\{0,\ldots,H_a-1\},\qquad
 C: \mathbb R^n\longrightarrow W,\qquad \deg C\le j.$$ Lower layers have already been substituted. Rank means the ordinary rank condition of Definition <a href="#sampling:rank" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:rank">85</a>, with the single tag $j$: no integer row of norm at most $R_j$, nonzero on $W$, takes the degree-$j$ symbol of $C$ to a slow-plus-rational polynomial at bound $R_j$. Warm, cold-pre, and late choices have the meanings fixed in Definition <a href="#ap:budgets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ap:budgets">5</a>. All degrees and cube orders below belong to a fixed finite range. Structural numbers of columns are polynomial in dimensions and are fixed before numerical precisions.

<a id="pm-h-21"></a>
#### Normalized lift charts

Put $\Lambda=W\cap\mathbb Z^d$ and $\Lambda'=\operatorname{proj}_{W^\perp}\mathbb Z^d$. Choose the basis $v_i$, $1\le i\le\dim W^\perp$, of the projected lattice $\Lambda'$ supplied by Lemma <a href="#sampling:lattice-chart" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:lattice-chart">88</a>, and set <a id="ap:path:mass"></a>$$\label{ap:path:mass}
 K_i=\max(1,\lceil |v_i|^{-1}\rceil),\qquad
 k_i=\max(1,\lceil K_i v\rceil),
 \qquad
 m_j=v^{\dim W}\frac{\prod_i k_i}{\mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda)}.$$ Here $v$ is a sufficiently small warm fraction of $w_j$. All lift coordinates use this same physical width. More precisely, $v/w_j$ has logarithmic cost polynomial in dimensions and $\log\gamma^{-1}$. Principal amplitudes in normalized lift units, and the proportionality constants in inactive side lengths, can have logarithmic costs depending only on dimensions. They are chosen small enough that all true and ideal lifts lie well inside a buffered chart of radius comparable to $v$, itself inside the required gap. These charts are narrow enough that every Boolean difference of an order used below has components of magnitude less than $1/2$.

For a center $c\in W/\Lambda$, choose a representative in $W$. On a uniqueness chart write $$C(u)-c=y(u)+\beta(u),\qquad \beta(u)\in\mathbb Z^d.$$ The sheet coordinates satisfy $$\operatorname{proj}_{W^\perp}y=\sum_i v_i z_i
       =-\operatorname{proj}_{W^\perp}\beta.$$ Choose integer lifts of the basis vectors $v_i$, and let $l(z)$ be their integer linear combination. Then $\beta+l(z)\in\Lambda$. Choose an integer basis of $\Lambda$ and let $w$ be the coordinates of $\beta+l(z)$ in that basis. Primitivity of $\Lambda$ shows that $\beta\mapsto(z,w)$ is an integer unimodular change of coordinates. Here $w$ is a deck coordinate, not a width. A residue character of $(z,w)$ is therefore a residue character of $\beta$ at the same modulus; the real size of the basis coefficients does not enter this assertion.

<a id="stmt-ap-path-chart"></a>
<div id="ap:path:chart" class="lemma">

**Lemma 6** (Chart mass and normalized coordinates). *The quantities $m_j$ and $m_j^{-1}$ have cold-pre bounds independent of the height of $W$. On a buffered chart the coordinates $y_W/v$ and $z_i/k_i$ have dimension-controlled norms in terms of $y/v$. The row defining $z_i$ on the ambient lift has norm at most $\exp(\operatorname{poly}(d))K_i$, is integral on $\mathbb Z^d$, and annihilates $W$.*

*A bounded warm enlargement of the chart has Haar measure at most a warm multiple of $m_j$. A ball of a warm fraction of radius $v$, centered at a feasible torus point and with the prescribed room, has Haar measure at least a warm inverse multiple of $m_j$. These relative bounds do not depend on any width when the radius ratios use only dimensions and $\gamma$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ap-path-chart"><summary>Proof of stmt-ap-path-chart</summary>

*Proof.* Lemma <a href="#sampling:lattice-chart" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sampling:lattice-chart">88</a> gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda)\asymp_{\exp(\operatorname{poly}(d))}\prod_iK_i$$ and dimension-controlled maps between the projected Euclidean coordinates and $z_i/K_i$. Since $k_i\asymp\max(1,K_i v)$, multiplying the latter coordinates by $K_i v/k_i\le1$ proves the asserted upper norm bound. The dual projected lattice is the integral annihilator of $W$, giving the integral rows and their stated norms. If $q=\dim W^\perp$, then $$\exp(-\operatorname{poly}(d))v^d
       \le m_j\le \exp(\operatorname{poly}(d))v^{\dim W}.$$ In particular its logarithmic costs involve $\log v^{-1}$ but not subspace height.

Haar measure in these coordinates is Lebesgue measure on $W$ times counting measure on the sheets, divided by $\mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda)$. Counting sheet coordinates in a dimension-controlled parallelepiped and integrating on $W$ gives the upper bound. Around a feasible sheet, a smaller such parallelepiped contains at least a dimension-controlled multiple of $\prod_i\max(1,\tau k_i)$ sheet points when its radius is $\tau v$; this is at least $\tau^q\prod_i k_i$ up to dimension factors. Integration on $W$ supplies the other $\tau^{\dim W}$ factor. This proves the lower bound, including arbitrary fixed real translations of the chart. Feasibility is necessary: no assertion is made that an arbitrary translated small box meets the torus. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-22"></a>
#### The coefficient law and the actual path ensemble

First consider the model $W=\mathbb R^d$, where there are no discrete sheet coordinates. We want the spatial directions and the small-lift directions to be recoverable separately. The reference lift law therefore uses disjoint blocks of $j$ parameters with a common side $L$, to be selected later. On a lift axis $a$, its principal part has the form $$\frac{y_a^{\rm ideal}(t)}v=\eta_a+
       \sum_B c_{aB}\prod_{\ell\in B}\frac{t_\ell}{L},$$ with the normalized $c_{aB}$ bounded away from zero. The constant $\eta_a$ supplies the local translation. The blocks for different axes are disjoint, and a separate kernel block controls the spatial image. Fixing all but one variable in each selected product at normalized values bounded away from zero gives independent directions in this ideal model. Repeating the products on further disjoint blocks also smooths their one-site and cube evaluation laws.

The reason to recover lift directions rather than raw integer coefficients comes from the lift identity we require. We will arrange that $C(\psi(t))-c=y(t)+\beta(t)$ is a polynomial identity of degree at most $j$. Its top homogeneous parts then give $$\beta_{[j]}(t)-C_{[j]}(\psi_{[1]}(t))=-y_{[j]}(t).$$ Here brackets denote ordinary homogeneous degree. Thus the products control the deviation of the integer variable from its prescribed polynomial value without any bound on the coefficients of $C$. Small remaining lift coefficients and small nonkernel spatial displacements perturb this ideal recovery map; they do not give exact independence to the full map.

For a rational $W$, the projected lift coordinates are integer sheets. Their available ranges determine whether the preceding products can use long parameters or must instead use coefficient one and shorter parameters. We now prescribe those ranges and the additional columns needed for residue tests and exact sheet translations. All independence in this prescription belongs to the reference coefficient law and the separate spatial law. The actual path law couples them by the tilt below.

After the pre requirements are fixed, choose a perturbation parameter $0<\sigma<1$ and a range parameter $A\ge2$, in that order. Rank thresholds and parent sides will be chosen later. Choose a scale gap with no $k_i^{1/j}$ between $L$ and $AL$. For example, among more than $\dim W^\perp$ consecutive disjoint multiplicative intervals of ratio $A$, at least one contains none of these numbers. Hence this choice is possible with $A\le L\le A^{O(1+d)}$. With a fixed sufficiently large degree-dependent $C_*$, call a sheet axis $$\begin{array}{ll}
 \text{inactive}& k_i\le L^j,\\
 \text{moderate}& (AL)^j\le k_i\le L^{C_*},\\
 \text{enormous}& k_i>L^{C_*}.
 \end{array}$$ There are only polynomially many numbers to avoid, so $\log L$ can be chosen with the permitted late bound without using their magnitudes. Rounding is performed with fixed buffers at the cutoffs. An active sheet axis means a moderate or enormous axis.

The parameter box is $\mathcal T=\prod_\ell\{0,\ldots,T_\ell-1\}$. We prescribe its columns, the independent reference law of the lift coefficients, and the supports of the separate spatial law as follows. The actual coefficients of $C(x+Vt)$ are determined by $(x,V)$; the tilt defined below combines these two laws.

1.  To keep the spatial image nondegenerate independently of the principal lift directions, spatial kernel columns have side $L$.
