The Gowers triangle inequality selects one, call it $Q$, such that $$\|f1_Q\|_{U^j(H)}\ge4^{-n}\|f\|_{U^j(H)}.$$ A two-face discrepancy with all vertices in this box has absolute value less than $2N_i/3$ in coordinate $i$. If it is zero modulo $N_i$, it is therefore zero as an integer. The group and integer cube sums agree, so $$\|f1_Q\|_{U^j(H)}^{2^j}
 =\frac{C_j(Q)}{|H|^{j+1}}\|f|_Q\|_{U^j(Q)}^{2^j}.$$ In particular the restricted box norm is at least $e^{-p}4^{-n}$. The box result gives a cap-one representative-coordinate niltest $T$ with $|\mathbb E_Q f\overline T|\ge\eta$, where $\eta\ge\exp(-\operatorname{poly}_s(p+n))$. Put $\lambda=(|Q|/|H|)\eta\ge8^{-n}\eta$.

We may insert a smooth selector without a lower bound on the cyclic moduli. For each nonsingleton cyclic coordinate, take the circle arc whose endpoints lie halfway between the grid points just inside and outside its selected interval. A $[0,1]$-valued Lipschitz approximation $W_i$ with transition radius $\theta$ and Lipschitz constant $O(\theta^{-1})$ has discrete $L^1$ error $O(\theta)$. Indeed, if $\theta<1/(2N_i)$ it agrees with the indicator on the grid; otherwise each transition interval contains $O(N_i\theta)$ grid points. For $N_i=1$ take $W_i=1$. The product selector $W=\prod_iW_i$ has error $O(n\theta)$. Choose $\theta$ so that this is at most $\lambda/4$. Then $$|\mathbb E_H f\overline{WT}|\ge3\lambda/4.$$ The selector is a degree-one niltest on an $n$-dimensional torus, and its logarithmic Lipschitz cost is polynomial in $p+n$. Thus $WT$ has degree at most $s$, cap one, and the required complexity and correlation. This completes the local extension.

For a subgroup $H\le G$, write $H^\Delta=\{(h,h):h\in H\}$ for its diagonal subgroup in $G\times G$.

The relative-square construction and its diagonal quotient occur in Green and Tao <a id="pm-cite-39"></a>[[GreenTaoOrbits2012](#ref-GreenTaoOrbits2012), Proposition 7.2 and Lemma 7.4]. We record the normalization and its quantitative coordinate proof here so that the number of parameters and the group dimension remain explicit.

<a id="stmt-prelim-square"></a>
<div id="prelim:square" class="lemma">

**Lemma 54** (Normalized square). *Let $F$ be vertical of frequency $\eta$ on $G_s$ and let $g$ be an adapted polynomial map. For a fixed integer shift $h$, after a constant right lattice translation and a bounded constant left translation of $g(t+h)$, the pair with $g(t)$ is polynomial in $$G^\square_j=G_j^\Delta(G_{j+1}\times G_{j+1}).$$ The function given by the product of the translated $F$ and $\overline F$ descends by $G_s^\Delta$. It is consequently a degree-$(s-1)$ niltest, of controlled complexity independent of the coefficients of $g$ and of $h$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prelim-square"><summary>Proof of stmt-prelim-square</summary>

*Proof.* The horizontal difference $g(t+h)g(t)^{-1}\bmod G_2$ is constant in $t$. Reduce it modulo the projected lattice. Thus choose $\gamma_h\in\Gamma$ and bounded $\epsilon_h\in G$ whose horizontal logarithms are $m_h,e_h$, respectively, and whose sum is this difference. The first path $\epsilon_h^{-1}g(t+h)\gamma_h^{-1}$ now has the same horizontal coordinate as the second path.

Put $d_h(t)=\epsilon_h^{-1}g(t+h)\gamma_h^{-1}g(t)^{-1}$. The logarithm of $d_h$, in original Lie layer $j$, has parameter degree at most $j-1$. In the finite Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff expansion, a term without a shift difference or inserted constant cancels, while either operation lowers parameter degree relative to Lie layer by at least one. The factorization $$(\epsilon_h^{-1}g(t+h)\gamma_h^{-1},g(t))
     =(d_h(t),1)(g(t),g(t))$$ therefore proves polynomiality in $G^\square_\bullet$. Right multiplication by $\gamma_h^{-1}$ leaves the original coset unchanged. The new function is $F(\epsilon_hx)\overline{F(y)}$; its Lipschitz bound depends on the bounded $\epsilon_h$ alone. Central equivariance cancels on $G_s^\Delta$. The final filtration layer is that diagonal group, so quotienting reduces the degree. All structural and metric bounds follow from the preceding rational operations; only the coefficients of the new orbit can be large. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-prelim-dual-gowers"></a>
<div id="prelim:dual-gowers" class="lemma">

**Lemma 55** (Niltests detect Gowers uniformity). *If a unit-bounded function on a box of dimension $\mathcal P(p)$ correlates by at least $e^{-p}$ with a degree-$s$ niltest of complexity $\mathcal P(p)$, then its $U^{s+1}$ norm is at least $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$. The assertion also holds on cyclic groups, including products of a bounded number of translated tests in representative coordinates.*

</div>

The interval case is the converse inverse theorem of Leng, Sah and Sawhney <a id="pm-cite-40"></a>[[LSSInverse2024](#ref-LSSInverse2024), Lemma B.5]. We give the box argument to keep its dependence on the number of parameters explicit.

<details id="proof-stmt-prelim-dual-gowers"><summary>Proof of stmt-prelim-dual-gowers</summary>

*Proof.* Induct on $s$, the case $s=0$ being the definition of $U^1$. Lemma <a href="#prelim:vertical" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:vertical">50</a> selects a top mode $T$, which we may rescale to be unit-bounded, with $\rho:=|\langle f,T\rangle_Q|\geq\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$. Put $a=f\overline T$ and $c_h=\mathbb E_{Q_h}\Delta_ha$. The exact identity is <a id="prelim:mean-square"></a>$$\label{prelim:mean-square}
 \rho^2=\sum_{h:Q_h\ne\varnothing}
               \frac{|Q_h|}{|Q|^2}c_h.$$ There are at most $2^n|Q|$ shifts. With $\tau=2^{-n-2}\rho^2$, overlaps of volume below $\tau|Q|$ contribute at most $\rho^2/4$ in absolute value. Discarding also $|c_h|<\rho^2/4$ leaves a total absolute contribution at least $\rho^2/2$. Each weight is at most $1/|Q|$, so at least $\rho^2|Q|/2$ shifts remain. Each retained overlap has volume at least $\tau|Q|$ and hence every side at least $\tau$ times its original side.

The product of the two mode values is the lower-degree niltest in Lemma <a href="#prelim:square" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:square">54</a>. Induction gives a lower bound $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$ for $\|\Delta_hf\|_{U^s(Q_h)}$ on every retained overlap. Inserting their count and volume bounds into <a href="#prelim:box-derivative" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:box-derivative">[prelim:box-derivative]</a>, and using the bounds for $C_s(Q_h)$, proves the assertion. All dimension factors are $\mathcal B(p)$.

In the cyclic case cut at every wrap point of the bounded number of translates and subdivide further into intervals of diameter less than $N/3$. This gives a bounded number of ordinary intervals. Select a piece retaining a controlled fraction of the correlation. Every cyclic cube supported on that piece has ordinary integer face identities, since a face discrepancy has magnitude less than $2N/3$ and is a multiple of $N$. Thus the integer and cyclic cube sums of its zero extension coincide, with the stated normalization factors. Finally a cutoff of an interval cannot convert a sufficiently small $U^j$ norm, $j\geq2$, into a large one at the present costs: smooth the cutoff with sufficiently small $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$ $L^1$ error and approximate it by a Fourier sum of $\mathcal B(p)$ total coefficient mass. Use character invariance and the triangle inequality, and bound the $U^j$ norm of a unit-bounded error by its $L^1$ norm to the power $1/2^j$. This transfers the conclusion back to the uncut cyclic function. ◻

</details>

<a id="prelim:step-drop-section"></a>
### Dropping the top frequency of a biased symbol

A biased top-frequency niltest need not have a slowly varying orbit: large rational coefficients may remain. We separate these contributions at the level of the homogeneous symbol, leaving a structured factor whose top layer is annihilated by the tested frequency.

The antecedents are Leng’s efficient equidistribution theorem <a id="pm-cite-41"></a>[[LengEquidistribution2023](#ref-LengEquidistribution2023), Theorem 4] and the degree-reduction results of Leng, Sah and Sawhney <a id="pm-cite-42"></a>[[LSSInverse2024](#ref-LSSInverse2024), Theorem 5.4 and Corollary 5.5]. Unequal side lengths already occur in Leng’s theorem. The proof here supplies the symbol formulation with bounds uniform in a growing number of parameters, retaining each side length throughout.

<a id="stmt-prelim-step-drop"></a>
<div id="prelim:step-drop" class="lemma">

**Lemma 56** (Step drop for symbols). *Fix $s\geq1$. Let $F(g(t)\Gamma)$ be a degree-$s$ niltest of complexity at most $p$, on a box with $n\leq p$ variables and sides $T_i$. Suppose $F$ is vertical of top frequency $\eta$ of height at most $e^p$, and $$\left|\mathbb E_tF(g(t)\Gamma)\right|\geq e^{-p}.$$ For $\min_iT_i\geq\mathcal B(p)$ sufficiently large, the symbol admits a factorization $X=EPR$, where $E$ is slow, $R$ is rational, and $\log P$ takes values in a graded rational Lie subalgebra $W$ of height $\mathcal B(p)$ such that $\eta(W_s)=0$.*

</div>

The proof inducts on the fixed degree rather than the group dimension. Differentiation gives many biased normalized squares, to which the lower-degree statement applies. After fixing their rational data, we obtain slow-plus-rational relations for derivatives of one common symbol. A lattice argument recovers such relations for each coordinate derivative; the remaining argument removes their slow and rational parts grade by grade.

<a id="pm-h-90"></a>
#### Recovering coordinate derivatives

The recovery step below involves the adjoint action of a symbol whose coefficients need not be bounded. Its identity diagonal blocks nevertheless force bounded vertical lattice directions to be determined by their horizontal coordinates. The following lemma makes this assertion quantitative at the actual, possibly unequal, side lengths.

<a id="stmt-prelim-lattice"></a>
<div id="prelim:lattice" class="lemma">

<a id="prelim:lattice-definition"></a>
<a id="prelim:lattice-lifts"></a>
<a id="prelim:lattice-derivatives"></a>
**Lemma 57** (Lattice extraction). *Let $1\leq n,m\leq\mathcal P(p)$, $0\leq a\leq m$, $T_i>0$, and $l,R,\delta^{-1}\leq\mathcal B(p)$, where $l$ is a positive integer, $R\geq1$ and $0<\delta\leq1$. Put $D_T=\operatorname{diag}(T_1,\ldots,T_n)$, and let $L$ be a positive diagonal $m\times m$ matrix. Its first $a$ entries equal $1$, and every remaining entry is at least $T_*:=\min_iT_i$. Let $M$ be lower unitriangular, with identity on its first $a\times a$ block, and let $Y:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ be any linear map. Suppose the lattice $$\label{prelim:lattice-definition}
 \Lambda=\{(D_T^{-1}h,L(Yh-Mr)):
             h\in\mathbb Z^n,\ r\in l^{-1}\mathbb Z^m\}$$ contains at least $\delta\prod_iT_i$ vectors of norm at most $R$ with distinct $h$-coordinates. No size bound is imposed on $M$ or $Y$. If $T_*\geq\mathcal B(p)$ is sufficiently large, there are a rational subspace $K\subseteq\mathbb R^a$ of height $\mathcal B(p)$ and linear maps $S,\mathcal R:K\to\mathbb R^m$ with $$\label{prelim:lattice-lifts}
 S=M\mathcal R,\qquad
 S(k)_{\mathrm{hor}}=\mathcal R(k)_{\mathrm{hor}}=k,
 \qquad |LS(k)|\leq\mathcal B(p)|k|.$$ On a controlled rational basis of $K$, $\mathcal R$ has a common denominator $\mathcal B(p)$, with no numerator bound. Moreover $$\label{prelim:lattice-derivatives}
 Ye_i=s_i+Mr_i+S(k_i),\qquad
 |Ls_i|\leq\mathcal B(p)/T_i,$$ where $k_i\in K$ and the $r_i$ have a common denominator $\mathcal B(p)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prelim-lattice"><summary>Proof of stmt-prelim-lattice</summary>

*Proof.* The map defining <a href="#prelim:lattice-definition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:lattice-definition">[prelim:lattice-definition]</a> is invertible on $\mathbb R^{n+m}$, so $\Lambda$ is a lattice. Let $Z$ be the span of its vectors of norm at most $R$, and put $\Lambda_Z=\Lambda\cap Z$. If their $h$-projections lay in a proper subspace, one nonzero real linear equation would determine one coordinate from the others. The number of integer possibilities would be at most $$(3R)^{n-1}\frac{\prod_iT_i}{T_*},$$ contrary to the hypothesis when $T_*$ is sufficiently large. Thus $Z$ projects onto $\mathbb R^n$.

Write $d=\dim Z$. There are $d$ independent lattice vectors of norm at most $R$ spanning $Z$. Their integral span has covering radius at most $dR/2$, by rounding real coefficients to integers. The larger lattice $\Lambda_Z$ has no larger covering radius. Its Voronoi fundamental region is consequently contained in a ball of radius $dR/2$. Translate that region by the given bounded lattice vectors. The translates are disjoint up to null sets and are contained in a ball of radius $(1+d/2)R$. Therefore <a id="prelim:lattice-covolume"></a>$$\label{prelim:lattice-covolume}
 \mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda_Z)\leq C_*/\prod_iT_i,
 \qquad
 C_*:=\delta^{-1}(C(n+m)R)^{C(n+m)},$$ for an absolute constant $C$.

<a id="prelim:lattice-product"></a>
Let $V=Z\cap(\{0\}\times\mathbb R^m)$ and $\Lambda_V=\Lambda\cap V$. The projection in unscaled $h$-coordinates is a full-rank subgroup $H\leq\mathbb Z^n$; put $I=[\mathbb Z^n:H]$. The lattice $\Lambda_V$ has full rank in $V$: the projection of a lattice basis of $\Lambda_Z$ is an integer matrix of rank $n$ in the unscaled $h$-coordinates, and its real kernel is spanned by rational, hence integral, kernel vectors. Orthogonally to $V$, the space $Z$ is the graph of a linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to V^\perp\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, whose input is the scaled coordinate $D_T^{-1}h$. Lift a basis of $D_T^{-1}H$ to $\Lambda_Z$ and subtract its $V$-components when calculating the exterior product with a basis of $\Lambda_V$. This gives the exact identity $$\mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda_Z)=
 \mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda_V)\frac{I}{\prod_iT_i}
 \sqrt{\det(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}+A^*A)}.$$ Writing $E_A=\sqrt{\det(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}+A^*A)}$, we obtain $$\label{prelim:lattice-product}
 \mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda_V)I E_A\leq C_*.$$ Every singular value of $x\mapsto(x,Ax)$ is at least one, so $|(x,Ax)|\leq E_A|x|$.

<a id="prelim:lattice-pivot"></a>
Put $k=\dim V$, and write a basis of the vertical lattice, after changing signs if necessary, as the columns of $LMR_b$, where $R_b\in(l^{-1}\mathbb Z)^{m\times k}$. Scan the rows of $R_b$ from top to bottom, retaining a row exactly when it increases the span. Let $J$ be the resulting $k$ pivot rows. Every earlier nonpivot row is a linear combination of earlier pivot rows. Hence multiplication by the lower unitriangular matrix $M$ changes the selected rows by a lower unitriangular row operation. In particular, $$\det(MR_b)_J=\det(R_b)_J.$$ If $w_j$ denotes the $j$th diagonal entry of $L$, Cauchy–Binet therefore gives $$\label{prelim:lattice-pivot}
 \mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda_V)\geq
 |\det(LMR_b)_J|
 =\Bigl(\prod_{j\in J}w_j\Bigr)|\det(R_b)_J|
 \geq l^{-k}\prod_{j\in J}w_j.$$ If any pivot were nonhorizontal, the last expression would be at least $l^{-k}T_*$. This contradicts <a href="#prelim:lattice-product" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:lattice-product">[prelim:lattice-product]</a> once $T_*>C_*l^m$. All pivots are horizontal. Thus horizontal projection is injective on $V$ and its image is a rational subspace $K\subseteq\mathbb R^a$. Equations <a href="#prelim:lattice-product" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:lattice-product">[prelim:lattice-product]</a>–<a href="#prelim:lattice-pivot" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:lattice-pivot">[prelim:lattice-pivot]</a> give $$I,E_A\leq C_*l^k,\qquad
 l^{-k}\leq\mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda_V)\leq C_*.$$

Let $H_b$ be the horizontal rows of $R_b$. They are also the horizontal rows of $LMR_b$. Every maximal minor of $H_b$ is bounded in absolute value by $C_*$, and belongs to $l^{-k}\mathbb Z$. Choose a nonzero maximal minor $(H_b)_{J_0}$. The columns of $H_b((H_b)_{J_0})^{-1}$ form a rational basis of $K$. Its entries are ratios of maximal minors, hence have controlled height. No short basis for $\Lambda_V$ is required here.

The unique graph lift from $K$ to $V$ has volume expansion $$\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(\Lambda_V)}{\mathop{\mathrm{covol}}(H_b\mathbb Z^k)}
 \leq C_*l^k.$$ As its horizontal part is the identity, its singular values are at least one and this also bounds its norm. Denote the lift by $k_0\mapsto LS(k_0)$, and define $$\mathcal R\bigl(H_b((H_b)_{J_0})^{-1}u\bigr)
 =R_b((H_b)_{J_0})^{-1}u.$$ Then $S=M\mathcal R$. The matrix on the right has denominator dividing the nonzero integer $\det(l(H_b)_{J_0})$, whose magnitude is at most $C_*l^k$. This proves <a href="#prelim:lattice-lifts" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:lattice-lifts">[prelim:lattice-lifts]</a>.

Finally $I\mathbb Z^n\subseteq H$. Lift $Ie_i$ to $\Lambda_Z$ and divide the lift by $I$. The resulting vector is $$(T_i^{-1}e_i,L(Ye_i-Mr'_i/I)),\qquad
 r'_i\in l^{-1}\mathbb Z^m.$$ Its component orthogonal to $V$ has norm at most $E_A/T_i$. Write that component’s vertical coordinate as $Ls_i$, and the $V$-component as $LS(k_i)$. Taking $r_i=r'_i/I$ proves <a href="#prelim:lattice-derivatives" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:lattice-derivatives">[prelim:lattice-derivatives]</a>. Its denominator divides $lI$. Zero-dimensional lattices have covolume one; the same argument, with empty bases, covers $k=0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-91"></a>
#### Proof of the step-drop lemma

<details id="proof-stmt-prelim-lattice-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-prelim-lattice</summary>

*Proof.* If $\eta=0$, take $W=\mathfrak n$ and $E=R=1$. A zero-variable symbol is also trivial, so assume that the box has at least one variable and that $\eta\ne0$. We induct on $s$. If $s=1$, the group is a vector group and verticality gives $F(x)=c\,e(\eta(x))$ with $|c|\leq e^p$. Choose a rational vector $v$ of controlled height with $\eta(v)=1$. Write $\log X(t)=\sum_i a_it_i$. The product formula for the mean of a linear phase and the geometric-sum bound give integers $q_i$ such that $$|\eta(a_i)-q_i|\leq e^{2p}/(2T_i).$$ Indeed the product of the $n$ normalized geometric sums has magnitude at least $e^{-2p}$, so each individual magnitude is at least $e^{-2p}$. Take slow coefficients $(\eta(a_i)-q_i)v$, rational coefficients $q_iv$, and middle coefficients in $\ker\eta$. This proves the base case.

<a id="pm-h-92"></a>
###### The differentiated symbol.

Assume $s\geq2$. Apply the weighted-shift selection in the proof of Lemma <a href="#prelim:dual-gowers" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:dual-gowers">55</a>, after rescaling $F$ to be unit-bounded. Together with Lemma <a href="#prelim:square" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:square">54</a>, it gives at least $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}\prod_iT_i$ distinct shifts $h$, with $|h_i|\leq T_i$, for which the normalized square test has a mean of magnitude at least $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$ on its overlap, and whose individual side lengths are at least $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}T_i$.

Write $\mathfrak n_j=\mathfrak g_j/\mathfrak g_{j+1}$. The associated graded Lie algebra of the quotient square has diagonal layers $\mathfrak n_j$, $1\leq j<s$, and relative layers $\mathfrak n_{j+1}$ in square degree $j$. The relative part is abelian in this associated graded algebra: the bracket of two relative inputs has one extra filtration degree. The diagonal acts on it by the ordinary adjoint action.

<a id="prelim:square-symbol"></a>
Use the normalization in Lemma <a href="#prelim:square" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:square">54</a>, writing $$(\log X)_1(h)=e_h+m_h,$$ where $e_h$ has controlled size and $m_h$ lies in a fixed rational grid. For a symbol $C$ write $Y_h(C)=(\partial_hC)C^{-1}$ for its right logarithmic derivative. In relative-then-diagonal semidirect coordinates, the square symbol is $$\label{prelim:square-symbol}
 \left(X_{\leq s-1},\,
       Y_h(X)-e_h-\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Xm_h\right).$$ Here the relative component in original layer $j$ is its homogeneous parameter part of degree $j-1$, and the horizontal part is zero. Here is a formal verification, including the case where the original filtration has no grading. Choose complements $E_j$ of $\mathfrak g_{j+1}$ in $\mathfrak g_j$ and let $\delta_z$ act by $z^j$ on $E_j$. The brackets $$[u,v]_z=\delta_z[\delta_z^{-1}u,\delta_z^{-1}v]$$ are polynomial in $z$: a component in $E_k$ of a bracket of $E_i,E_j$ is multiplied by $z^{k-i-j}$, with $k\geq i+j$. At $z=0$ this is the associated graded bracket. Write $\exp_z,\log_z$ for the finite Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff group with this bracket. The polynomial $$P_z(t)=\delta_z\log g(t/z)$$ has constant term $P_0(t)=\log X(t)$. Similarly the scaled normalizing constants are $ze_h+O(z^2)$ and $zm_h+O(z^2)$. Here $O(z^2)$ denotes terms divisible by $z^2$ in a formal polynomial, without any bound on their coefficients. The scaled relative product is therefore $$\exp_z(-ze_h+O(z^2))\exp_z(P_z(t+zh))
 \exp_z(-zm_h+O(z^2))\exp_z(-P_z(t)).$$ When the shift and inserted constants are zero, the middle product equals the identity for every $z$. Consequently the first-order variations of the bracket itself and of the subleading coefficients in $P_z$ cancel identically. The coefficient of $z$ depends only on the displayed shift and insertions, evaluated in the graded group at $z=0$. It can thus be calculated over the dual numbers $\mathbb R[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$, where the exact identity is $$\exp(-\varepsilon e_h)X(t+\varepsilon h)
 \exp(-\varepsilon m_h)X(t)^{-1}
 =\exp\!\left(\varepsilon
       (Y_h(X)-e_h-\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Xm_h)\right).$$ Indeed $X(t+\varepsilon h)X(t)^{-1}=\exp(\varepsilon Y_h(X))$, conjugation of the right insertion gives $\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Xm_h$, and brackets of two $\varepsilon$ terms vanish. In original layer $j$, the coefficient of $z$ is exactly the homogeneous parameter part of degree $j-1$ of the relative logarithm, since $\delta_z$ multiplies that monomial by $z^{j-(j-1)}$. This proves <a href="#prelim:square-symbol" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:square-symbol">[prelim:square-symbol]</a>. The same calculation gives the semidirect multiplication rule $y+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Xy'$ under a preceding diagonal coordinate $X$.

<a id="pm-h-93"></a>
###### A common fast subgroup.

Apply Lemma <a href="#prelim:vertical" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:vertical">50</a> to the quotient square. One top mode retains bias $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$, and its restriction to the relative copy of $\mathfrak n_s$ is $\eta$. The induction hypothesis factors its symbol into slow, fast and rational factors. Every resulting fast subalgebra has polynomial dimension and rational height $\mathcal B(p)$. There are only $\mathcal B(p)$ possibilities, since a rational basis is specified by polynomially many bounded-height entries. Retain a set of $\mathcal B(p)^{-1}\prod_iT_i$ shifts with the same fast subalgebra $\widetilde U$.

<a id="prelim:UV"></a>
Let $U$ be its diagonal projection, with $U_s=\mathfrak n_s$, and let $V_j\subseteq\mathfrak n_j$ be its kernel in the relative part, setting $V_1=0$. Then $$\label{prelim:UV}
 \eta(V_s)=0,\qquad [U_i,V_j]\subseteq V_{i+j}.$$ All these are controlled rational spaces. For each retained shift, denote the diagonal splitting by $X=A_hB_hD_h$ through grade $s-1$. Fix one retained shift and denote its outside diagonal factors by $A,D$. Lemma <a href="#prelim:symbol-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:symbol-splitting">52</a> puts $A^{-1}A_h$ and $D_hD^{-1}$ in $U$. Lift their logarithms to $\widetilde U$ by a bounded rational section of the diagonal projection. The first lift is slow, and the second is rational. Absorbing them into the middle factor makes its diagonal equal to $$B=A^{-1}XD^{-1}$$ for every retained shift. Extend $A,D$ to original grade $s$ with zero logarithmic component there; the same formula defines the full symbol $B$ and puts it in $U$.

<a id="prelim:common-derivative"></a>
In a subgroup of a semidirect product with abelian kernel, two elements with the same diagonal have relative coordinates equal modulo the kernel. The fast relative coordinate, denoted $Z_B$, is therefore common modulo $V$. Comparing the relative coordinates in <a href="#prelim:square-symbol" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:square-symbol">[prelim:square-symbol]</a> and using $$Y_h(ABD)=Y_h(A)+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_A Y_h(B)+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_{AB}Y_h(D)$$ gives $$\label{prelim:common-derivative}
 Y_h(B)=s_h+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Br_h+Z_B\pmod V.$$ For clarity, if $u_h,Z_h,v_h$ are the three relative factors, the two sides before solving for $Y_h(B)$ are $$Y_h(X)-e_h-\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Xm_h
       =u_h+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_AZ_h+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_{AB}v_h.$$ Thus one can take $$\begin{split}
 s_h&=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_{A^{-1}}(e_h+u_h-Y_h(A)),\\
 r_h&=v_h+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Dm_h-Y_h(D).
 \end{split}$$ The coefficients of $s_h$ in original layer $j$, parameter degree $j-1$, satisfy $\mathcal B(p)T^{-\alpha}$ bounds. This uses $|h_i|\leq T_i$ when differentiating the slow symbol $A$. The coefficients of $r_h$ have bounded denominator; integrality of $h$ is used for $Y_h(D)$. These claims include the horizontal constant terms. Pigeonhole the denominators and subtract one retained instance of <a href="#prelim:common-derivative" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:common-derivative">[prelim:common-derivative]</a> from every other instance. The term $Z_B$ disappears, the number of distinct shift differences is unchanged up to one, and the side and coefficient bounds only change by controlled factors.

<a id="pm-h-94"></a>
###### Extraction of a horizontal kernel.

Let $\mathcal M$ be the direct sum, over $j=1,\ldots,s$, of the coefficient spaces of degree-$(j-1)$ homogeneous polynomials with values in $\mathfrak n_j/V_j$. Choose controlled rational coordinates. The operator $M=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_B$ on $\mathcal M$ is block lower unitriangular by Lie layer, and is well defined by <a href="#prelim:UV" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:UV">[prelim:UV]</a>. The linear map $h\mapsto Y_h(B)$ takes values in $\mathcal M$. Let $L_T$ multiply a coefficient of $t^\alpha$ by $T^\alpha$. The horizontal scales are one and every other scale is at least $\min_iT_i$.

<a id="prelim:derivative-system"></a>
The subtracted identities supply the bounded lattice vectors required by Lemma <a href="#prelim:lattice" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:lattice">57</a>, with a common grid for the $r_h$; changing from the chosen rational coordinates to a rectangular grid merely enlarges its denominator. Consequently there are a controlled rational $K\subseteq\mathfrak n_1$, linear maps $S,R$ on $K$, and, for every coordinate derivative, $$\label{prelim:derivative-system}
 \begin{split}
 &S=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_B R\pmod V,\qquad S(k)_1=R(k)_1=k,\\
 &|L_TS(k)|\leq\mathcal B(p)|k|,\\
 &Y_i(B)=s_i+\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Br_i+S(k_i)\pmod V,\qquad
 |L_Ts_i|\leq\mathcal B(p)/T_i.
 \end{split}$$ Here $R$ on a controlled rational basis and all the $r_i$ have bounded common denominator, and $k_i\in K$ need not be rational. We henceforth use these identities in the quotient coefficient space, so equalities of components are always interpreted modulo $V_j$.

<a id="pm-h-95"></a>
###### The target subalgebra.

We have obtained the derivative system <a href="#prelim:derivative-system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:derivative-system">[prelim:derivative-system]</a>, with $B$ taking values in $U$. Define $$W_1=\{v\in K\cap U_1:[v,K]\subseteq V_2\},\qquad
 W_j=V_j\cap U_j\quad(2\leq j\leq s).$$ These controlled rational spaces form a graded Lie subalgebra. Indeed $[W_1,W_1]\subseteq V_2\cap U_2$, while every other required bracket lies in the appropriate $U$ layer and in $V$ by <a href="#prelim:UV" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:UV">[prelim:UV]</a>. Also $\eta(W_s)=0$. It remains to remove slow and rational factors from $B$ until its logarithmic coefficients lie in $W$.

Write $P_j=(\log B)_j$, updating this notation after each removal. First we put $P_1$ in $U_1\cap K$. At stage $j\ge2$ we arrange $[P_{j-1},K]\subseteq V_j$ and then put $P_j$ in $U_j\cap V_j$. The accompanying derivative terms must vanish at the same time so that the next layer reduces to an ordinary coefficient equation. We begin with the two operations that preserve the derivative system.

<a id="pm-h-96"></a>
###### Removing slow and rational derivatives.

<a id="prelim:transformation"></a>
<a id="prelim:absorption"></a>
The system <a href="#prelim:derivative-system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:derivative-system">[prelim:derivative-system]</a> is preserved when $B=aB'b$, where $a$ is slow and $b$ rational, both in $U$. The correct transformed quantities are $$\label{prelim:transformation}
 \begin{aligned}
 S'&=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_{a^{-1}}S,& R'&=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_b R,\\
 s'_i&=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_{a^{-1}}(s_i-Y_i(a)),&
 r'_i&=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_b r_i-Y_i(b).
 \end{aligned}$$ The identities follow from the product rule for $Y_i$. Their quantitative bounds persist: after coefficient scaling by $T^\alpha$, multiplication by a slow coefficient only multiplies norms by a controlled factor; rational products preserve bounded denominators. Also, for $k_s,k_r\in K$, the replacement $$\label{prelim:absorption}
 s_i\leftarrow s_i-S(k_s),\qquad
 r_i\leftarrow r_i-R(k_r),\qquad
 k_i\leftarrow k_i+k_s+k_r$$ preserves the system. Its bounds persist if $|k_s|\leq\mathcal B(p)/T_i$ and $k_r$ has bounded denominator.

<a id="prelim:horizontal-normalization"></a>
The coefficient of $t_i$ in $P_1$ is $s_{i,1}+r_{i,1}+k_i\in U_1$. Modulo the rational space $U_1+K$, separation puts $s_{i,1}$ and $r_{i,1}$ separately in that space. Use a controlled rational decomposition into a $U_1$ part and a $K$ part. Absorb the $K$ parts by <a href="#prelim:absorption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:absorption">[prelim:absorption]</a>, and remove the $U_1$ parts by factors $a,b$ whose logarithms have only layer one. We have arranged $$\label{prelim:horizontal-normalization}
 P_1\in U_1\cap K,\qquad s_{i,1}=r_{i,1}=0.$$

<a id="prelim:bracket-system"></a>
We now process $j=2,\ldots,s$. At the start of stage $j$, suppose the following hold: $$\begin{array}{ll}
 P_d\in U_d\cap V_d &(2\leq d<j),\\
 {}[P_d,K]\subseteq V_{d+1}&(1\leq d\leq j-2),\\
 S_d=R_d=0 &(2\leq d<j),\\
 s_{i,d}=r_{i,d}=0 &(1\leq d<j).
 \end{array}$$ The last two lines are statements in the quotient by $V$. Expanding $S=\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_B R$ in layer $j$ gives $$\label{prelim:bracket-system}
 [P_{j-1},k]=S_j(k)-R_j(k)\pmod {V_j},
 \qquad k\in K.$$ Indeed all lower terms of $R$ except its horizontal part vanish modulo $V$, and every term in $\exp(\operatorname{ad}P)k$ with an inner bracket from a layer at most $j-2$ belongs to $V$.

Let $E=U_{j-1}\cap V_{j-1}$, or $E=U_1\cap K$ when $j=2$. On a fixed controlled rational basis $(k_b)$ of $K$, define the rational linear map $$Q_j:E\longrightarrow\bigoplus_b\mathfrak n_j/V_j,
 \qquad v\longmapsto([v,k_b])_b.$$ The right side of <a href="#prelim:bracket-system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:bracket-system">[prelim:bracket-system]</a> is a slow coefficient array minus a rational one. Project modulo $Q_j(E)$, and apply Lemma <a href="#prelim:separation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:separation">51</a> coefficient by coefficient. Each part lies separately in the image. A controlled rational section provides homogeneous polynomials $a_{j-1},b_{j-1}$ with values in $E$ such that $$Q_j(a_{j-1})=(S_j(k_b))_b,\qquad
 Q_j(b_{j-1})=-(R_j(k_b))_b.$$ The first is slow and the second rational. Remove their exponentials from the left and right of $B$. Formula <a href="#prelim:transformation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:transformation">[prelim:transformation]</a> now gives $$[P_{j-1},K]\subseteq V_j,\qquad S_j=R_j=0.$$ Lower vanishing conditions persist. When $j=2$, the operation creates horizontal parts $-\partial_i a_1$ and $-\partial_i b_1$ in $s_i,r_i$; both lie in $K$. Absorb them by <a href="#prelim:absorption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:absorption">[prelim:absorption]</a>. Since the new $S_2,R_2$ are already zero modulo $V_2$, this restores <a href="#prelim:horizontal-normalization" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:horizontal-normalization">[prelim:horizontal-normalization]</a> without changing their vanishing. For $j>2$, the analogous new parts lie in $V_{j-1}$ and are already zero in the quotient.

At this point the right logarithmic derivative satisfies $$Y_i(B)_j=\partial_iP_j\pmod {V_j}.$$ To verify this, expand it as a finite sum of nested brackets of $P$ and $\partial_iP$. A derivative in a preceding layer at least two lies in $V$. A horizontal derivative lies in $K$, and its innermost bracket lies in $V$ by the bracket conditions just established. Subsequent brackets preserve $V$ by <a href="#prelim:UV" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:UV">[prelim:UV]</a>. Likewise $(\mathop{\mathrm{Ad}}_Br_i)_j=r_{i,j}$ modulo $V_j$, since all its lower components are already zero there. Thus <a href="#prelim:derivative-system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prelim:derivative-system">[prelim:derivative-system]</a> reduces to $$\partial_iP_j=s_{i,j}+r_{i,j}\pmod {V_j}.$$ For every monomial $t^\beta$ of degree $j$, choose one $i$ with $\beta_i>0$ and divide the corresponding derivative coefficient by $\beta_i$. This expresses its coefficient, modulo $V_j$, as a slow part of size $\mathcal B(p)T^{-\beta}$ and a rational part. Because $P_j$ takes values in $U_j$, separation modulo $U_j+V_j$ and a bounded rational section allow both parts to be lifted into $U_j$. Remove their exponential lifts at layer $j$. We have obtained $P_j\in U_j\cap V_j$. The derivative identity then says $s_{i,j}+r_{i,j}=0$ modulo $V_j$; separation, now at scale $T_iT^\alpha$, makes the two terms vanish separately. This completes stage $j$.

The final logarithmic coefficients now lie in the target algebra $W$, whose top layer is annihilated by $\eta$. There were only $s$ stages, with joint rational linear algebra at each stage. All corrections therefore combine into slow and rational outside factors with the stated bounds. Together with the original $A,D$, these give the required factorization of $X$. ◻

</details>

<a id="shift:section"></a>
### Shift comparison

Shift comparison lowers the degree of a positive test after multiplying by a translate of an arbitrary nonnegative function. The degree-one case uses Bohr-set almost-periodicity. At higher degree we recover the test from two fixed finite lists and apply the induction outside one exceptional set of shifts. The lower-degree test may then depend on the shift.

Put $G=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, with its uniform probability measure, and evaluate nilsequences on the representatives $0,\ldots,N-1$. For $d\geq 0$ and $q\geq2$, let $\mathcal T_d(q)$ denote the $[0,1]$-valued niltests of degree at most $d$ and complexity at most $q$. Thus $\mathcal T_0(q)$ consists of constants in $[0,1]$.

<a id="stmt-shift-required"></a>
<div id="shift:required" class="theorem">

<a id="shift:upper-hypothesis"></a>
<a id="shift:required-conclusion"></a>
**Theorem 58** (Shift comparison). *For fixed $d\geq1$ and $0<\epsilon<1$, there is a constant $C=C(d,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds. Suppose that $p\geq2$, $N\geq\exp((2+p)^C)$ is odd, and $0\leq f,g,J\leq e^p$. Set $P=(2+p)^C$. If $$\label{shift:upper-hypothesis}
 \mathbb E_n(f-g)(n)T(n)\leq e^{-P}
 \qquad(T\in\mathcal T_d(P)),$$ then there is a set $E\subseteq G$, depending on $f,g,J$, with $|E|\leq e^{-p}N$, such that $$\label{shift:required-conclusion}
 \mathbb E_n\bigl(f-(1+\epsilon)g\bigr)(n)J(n+h)T'(n)\leq e^{-p}
 \qquad(h\notin E,\ T'\in\mathcal T_{d-1}(p)).$$ The exceptional set is chosen before $T'$.*

</div>

The proof is given in Proposition <a href="#shift:degree-one" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:degree-one">63</a> for $d=1$ and Proposition <a href="#shift:higher" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:higher">69</a> for higher degrees. The latter uses the structural results of Section <a href="#prelim:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:section">12</a> and Lemma <a href="#prelim:step-drop" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:step-drop">56</a>.

<a id="pm-h-98"></a>
#### The degree-one argument

<a id="shift:bohr-tv"></a>
For a finite set $\Omega$ of characters of $G$ and $0<w\le1$, put $$B(\Omega,w)=\{x\in G:|\chi(x)-1|\le w\text{ for every }\chi\in\Omega\}.$$ We use these symmetric common-width Bohr sets, retaining $\Omega$ and $w(B)=w$ as part of the data; their rank is $D=|\Omega|$. The whole group has the presentation with one trivial character and width one. A regular Bohr set $B$ of rank $D\geq1$ satisfies $$|B_{1+t}|=(1+O(D|t|))|B|\qquad (|t|\leq c/D).$$ Here dilating a Bohr set means dilating its defining widths. The usual covering argument gives $|B|/N\geq(w(B)/10)^D$ and $|B_\rho|\geq(\rho/C)^{CD}|B|$ for $0<\rho<1$; a regular dilate exists between any two scales whose ratio is two. Also, if $v\in B_\rho$, regularity gives $$\label{shift:bohr-tv}
 \|\mu_B(\cdot-v)-\mu_B\|_1\ll D\rho,$$ Here $\mu_B(x)=1_B(x)/|B|$ is the probability mass function on $B$, and the norm in <a href="#shift:bohr-tv" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:bohr-tv">[shift:bohr-tv]</a> is the unnormalized sum over $G$. Regular dilation and the following almost-periodicity input preserve the common-width convention. Widths will be tracked explicitly; adding characters does not permit a width-independent estimate for the relative size of the resulting Bohr set.

The convolution almost-periodicity method originates with Croot and Sisask <a id="pm-cite-43"></a>[[CrootSisask2010](#ref-CrootSisask2010)]. We use the following radius-sensitive Bohr-set form of Schoen and Sisask.

<a id="stmt-shift-ap-width"></a>
<div id="shift:ap-width" class="lemma">

<a id="shift:ap-cost"></a>
**Lemma 59** (Almost-periodicity with a width bound). *Fix $0<\eta<1/2$. If $S,S'$ are regular of rank $D\geq1$, $A_1\subseteq S$, $A_2\subseteq s_0+S'$, both relative densities are at least $e^{-q}$ with $q\geq1$, and $|K|\leq2|S|$, then, for independent uniform $a_i\in A_i$, the probability that $a_1-a_2$ belongs to $K$ changes by at most $\eta$ after adding an independent uniform element of a regular Bohr set $D_*\subseteq S'$ with $$\label{shift:ap-cost}
 \mathop{\mathrm{rank}}D_*\leq D+C_\eta(1+q)^4,\qquad
 w(D_*)\geq w(S')\exp\bigl(-C_\eta(1+q+\log(2+D))\bigr).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-ap-width"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-ap-width</summary>

*Proof.* We apply Schoen–Sisask <a id="pm-cite-44"></a>[[SchoenSisask2016](#ref-SchoenSisask2016), Theorem 5.4], which uses unnormalized counting convolution. In its notation, a regular Bohr set of rank $d$ and radius $\rho$, a subset of relative density greater than $\sigma$, a sumset bound $|A+S_0|\leq K_1|A|$, and $\beta=|M|/|L|\leq1$ give a regular sub-Bohr set of rank at most $d+d'$ and radius at least $c\rho\eta\sqrt\beta/(d^2d')$, where $$d'\leq C\eta^{-2}\log^2(2/(\eta\beta))
       \log(2/\beta)\log(2K_1)+C\log(1/\sigma).$$ The error in its three-fold convolution is at most $\eta|A||M|$.

Write $\alpha_i$ for the two relative densities, and take a regular $B_0=S'_\tau$ with $\tau\asymp1/D$ sufficiently small. Use $B_0$ as the ambient Bohr set, and set $A=-A_2$, $S_0=B_0$. The increment set $S_0$ has density one in $B_0$, so $\sigma=1/2$ is valid; regularity gives $|A+S_0|\leq2|S'|\leq(2/\alpha_2)|A|$. If $|K|\geq|A_1|$, take $M=A_1$, $L=-K$; then $\alpha_1/2\leq\beta\leq1$. If $\eta|A_1|\leq|K|<|A_1|$, interchange $M$ and $L$; then $\eta\leq\beta\leq1$, and the error is still at most $\eta|A_1||A_2|$. In either case $d'\leq C_\eta(1+q)^4$, and the radius lower bound implies <a href="#shift:ap-cost" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:ap-cost">[shift:ap-cost]</a>. The counting convolution at zero, divided by $|A_1||A_2|$, is the probability in the statement; symmetry of $D_*$ gives the asserted smoothing estimate. Finally, if $|K|<\eta|A_1|$, every translate of the difference law assigns $K$ probability at most $|K|/|A_1|<\eta$. Taking $D_*=B_0$ proves this case as well. ◻

</details>

Only fixed $\eta>0$ is used here. All convolution normalizations in the following local calculation are stated explicitly.

<a id="stmt-shift-bilinear"></a>
<div id="shift:bilinear" class="lemma">

<a id="shift:bilinear-bound"></a>
**Lemma 60** (A bilinear reduction). *Let $a=f-(1+\epsilon)g$. In degree one it suffices to prove $$\label{shift:bilinear-bound}
 \mathbb E_{x,y}H(x)W(y)a(x+y)\leq e^{-4p}
 \qquad(0\leq H,W\leq1).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-bilinear"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-bilinear</summary>

*Proof.* If the conclusion fails on a set $E$ of more than $e^{-p}N$ shifts, then $\mathbb E_n a(n)J(n+h)>e^{-p}$ for every $h\in E$: a constant test cannot create a positive violation where this inequality fails. Take $H= e^{-p}J$ and $W(y)=1_E(-y)$. The left side of <a href="#shift:bilinear-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:bilinear-bound">[shift:bilinear-bound]</a> equals $e^{-p}\mathbb E_h1_E(h)\mathbb E_n a(n)J(n+h)>e^{-3p}$, a contradiction. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-99"></a>
###### The refinement to be proved.

To prove the bilinear estimate, we decompose its two independent averages into smaller Bohr cells. The difficulty is that a restriction can concentrate either weight. We measure both weights by a concave potential, so that concentration and genuine smoothing each pay for the further restrictions they require.

Write $a=f-(1+\epsilon)g$. A node consists of a regular Bohr set $B$, two translates $x_B+B,y_B+B$, and functions $H,W\in[0,1]$ supported on these translates. Define $$I=\mathbb E_{x\in x_B+B,\,y\in y_B+B}H(x)W(y)a(x+y),
 \enspace u=\mathbb E_{x\in x_B+B}H(x),
 \enspace v=\mathbb E_{y\in y_B+B}W(y),
 \enspace \Phi=(uv)^{1/4}.$$ Every node average uses the full size of its cell, even after a weight has been restricted and extended by zero. In particular, $I\le e^puv\le e^p\Phi$. The original bilinear average is the node with $B=G$.

<a id="shift:one-round-refinement"></a>
<a id="shift:one-round-geometry"></a>
We shall construct a refinement with successor nodes indexed by $\nu$ and nonnegative coefficients $c_\nu$ such that $$\label{shift:one-round-refinement}
 I\le\sum_\nu c_\nu I_\nu+\varepsilon_{\rm err}\Phi,
 \qquad
 \sum_\nu c_\nu\Phi_\nu\le(1-\gamma)\Phi.$$ Here $\gamma>0$ depends only on $\epsilon$, and $\varepsilon_{\rm err}$ can be any sufficiently small fixed multiple of $e^{-10p}$. Terms which need no further refinement are included in the error in the first inequality. The same construction controls the geometry: if $D$ and $w$ are the parent’s stored rank and width, every successor has $$\label{shift:one-round-geometry}
 D_\nu\le D+(2+p)^{A_\epsilon},\qquad
 \log\frac{w}{w_\nu}\le(2+p+D)^{B_\epsilon}.$$ We need this refinement only for descendants of the root during $R=\lceil c_{\rm depth}p\rceil$ rounds. The geometric bounds above forecast polynomial upper bounds for the ranks and $\log(1/w)$ of these nodes and their intermediate dilates. Choose $P$ to cover those bounds; the refinement is then uniform over every center and pair of weights encountered in the run.

There are two reasons to stop part of a node. If either cell mean is tiny, its entire positive contribution is small relative to $\Phi$. If a localized convolution is close to $1$ in a sufficiently high moment, positive comparison with a smooth Bohr test makes that localized contribution small. The other parts become successors. A highly concentrated restriction is paid for by the potential lost when that restriction is removed. In the absence of such concentration, a large convolution moment yields almost-periods and forces a fixed decrease of the average potential. The following two elementary estimates quantify these last two mechanisms.

<a id="stmt-shift-potential"></a>
<div id="shift:potential" class="lemma">

**Lemma 61** (Potential estimates). *Put $\theta=1/4$. The following estimates hold.*

<a id="shift:peeling"></a>
1.  *If $u,v>0$, $0\leq bu_1\leq u$, and $u_1\geq Ku$, then $$\label{shift:peeling}
     (uv)^\theta-((u-bu_1)v)^\theta
     \geq \theta K^{1-\theta}b(u_1v)^\theta.$$*

2.  *If $0\leq X\leq M$, $\mathbb EX\leq1$, and $\mathbb EX^2\geq1+c$, where $M\geq1$, then <a id="shift:concavity"></a>$$\label{shift:concavity}
     \mathbb E\sqrt X\leq1-\frac{c}{2(1+\sqrt M)^2}.$$ Consequently, if $X,Y\geq0$, $\mathbb EX,\mathbb EY\leq1$, and $X$ satisfies these additional bounds, then $\mathbb E(XY)^{1/4}\leq1-c/[4(1+\sqrt M)^2]$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-potential"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-potential</summary>

*Proof.* Concavity gives $1-(1-t)^\theta\geq\theta t$ for $0\leq t\leq1$. Apply this with $t=bu_1/u$, and use $(u_1/u)^{1-\theta}\geq K^{1-\theta}$. For the second assertion, $$\frac{1+x}{2}-\sqrt{x}
 =\frac{(x-1)^2}{2(1+\sqrt{x})^2}
 \geq\frac{(x-1)^2}{2(1+\sqrt M)^2}.$$ Moreover $\mathbb E(X-1)^2\geq c$ and $(1+\mathbb EX)/2\leq1$. The final assertion follows from Cauchy–Schwarz and $\mathbb E\sqrt Y\leq1$. ◻

</details>

The local moment argument and the weighted dependent-random-choice step below adapt the moment and sifting methods of Kelley and Meka <a id="pm-cite-45"></a>[[KelleyMeka2023](#ref-KelleyMeka2023), Sections 4–5], as developed in Bloom and Sisask <a id="pm-cite-46"></a>[[BloomSisaskKelleyMeka](#ref-BloomSisaskKelleyMeka), Sections 2.1–2.2]. Here they are used inside the refinement of two weighted Bohr cells.

<a id="stmt-shift-local-moments"></a>
<div id="shift:local-moments" class="lemma">

<a id="shift:flat"></a>
<a id="shift:unbalanced"></a>
**Lemma 62** (Local convolution alternatives). *Let $L,S$ be symmetric regular Bohr sets, with $S$ a sufficiently small dilate of $L$. Let $F,G\geq0$ be supported on $L$, have $|L|^{-1}\sum F=|L|^{-1}\sum G=1$, and satisfy $F,G\leq M$. Define $$(F*G)(t)=\frac1{|L|}\sum_xF(x)G(t-x),\qquad
 (F\circ G)(t)=\frac1{|L|}\sum_xF(x+t)G(x).$$ Write $\nu_+$ for the law of $s_1+s_2$ and $\nu_-$ for the law of $s_1-s_2$, where $s_1,s_2$ are independent and uniform on $S$. For fixed $\delta>0$, and integer $m\geq1$, either $$\label{shift:flat}
 \|F*G-1\|_{L^{2m}(\nu_+)}\leq\delta,$$ or, for one of $D=F,G$ and an integer $m'\leq C_\delta m$, $$\label{shift:unbalanced}
 \|D\circ D\|_{L^{2m'}(\nu_-)}\geq1+c_\delta.$$ It is enough that the regularity errors, multiplied by $M$, be sufficiently small in terms of $\delta$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-local-moments"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-local-moments</summary>

<a id="shift:moment-cs"></a>
<a id="shift:positive-moments"></a>
*Proof.* For real $A,B$ and every integer $j\geq1$, expansion and Cauchy–Schwarz give $$\label{shift:moment-cs}
 \|A*B\|_{L^{2j}(\nu_+)}
 \leq
 \|A\circ A\|_{L^{2j}(\nu_-)}^{1/2}
 \|B\circ B\|_{L^{2j}(\nu_-)}^{1/2}.$$ Indeed, after expanding the $2j$th power, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the two factors $\mathbb E_{s\in S}\prod_{i=1}^{2j}A(s-t_i)$ and $\mathbb E_{s\in S}\prod_{i=1}^{2j}B(s+t_i)$, summing each $t_i$ over the group with weight $|L|^{-1}$. The same expansion shows $$\label{shift:positive-moments}
 \mathbb E_{\nu_-}(A\circ A)^j\geq0\qquad(j\geq1),$$ because the resulting expression is a sum of squares.

Put $F_1=F-1_L$. Regularity and the cap $M$ show, uniformly on $S+S$ and $S-S$, respectively, that $$1_L*G=1+o_\delta(1),\qquad
 F\circ F=1+F_1\circ F_1+o_\delta(1).$$ If <a href="#shift:flat" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:flat">[shift:flat]</a> fails, then $\|F_1*G\|_{L^{2m}(\nu_+)}\geq\delta/2$. Either $\|G\circ G\|_{L^{2m}(\nu_-)}\geq2$, or <a href="#shift:moment-cs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:moment-cs">[shift:moment-cs]</a> gives $\|F_1\circ F_1\|_{L^{2m}(\nu_-)}\geq\delta^2/8$. In the latter case put $X=F_1\circ F_1$ and choose $m'=Rm$ with a sufficiently large integer $R=R(\delta)$. All terms in the binomial expansion have nonnegative expectations by <a href="#shift:positive-moments" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:positive-moments">[shift:positive-moments]</a>; hence $$\mathbb E(1+X)^{2m'}
 \geq \binom{2m'}{2m}\mathbb EX^{2m}
 \geq(R\delta^2/8)^{2m}.$$ Choose $R$ so that $(R\delta^2/8)^{1/R}>1+2c_\delta$, and absorb the uniform regularity error using the triangle inequality. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-shift-degree-one"></a>
<div id="shift:degree-one" class="proposition">

**Proposition 63** (Degree-one shift comparison). *Theorem <a href="#shift:required" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:required">58</a> holds for $d=1$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-degree-one"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-degree-one</summary>

*Proof.* We construct the refinement in <a href="#shift:one-round-refinement" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:one-round-refinement">[shift:one-round-refinement]</a>, with the geometry in <a href="#shift:one-round-geometry" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:one-round-geometry">[shift:one-round-geometry]</a> and the full-cell averaging convention fixed above. Put $\theta=1/4$.

Fix $K$ so large that $\theta K^{1-\theta}>2$, and choose $c_0>0$ with $(c_0K)^\theta\leq1/2$. Choose $\kappa=e^{-c_{\rm cut}p}$ and $\zeta=\exp(-(2+p)^{C_\epsilon'})$ sufficiently small. Choose $c_{\rm cut}=c_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)$ first to control the tiny-node error below. The moment constant and the number of rounds will be chosen afterwards; all are independent of the node rank. If $\min(u,v)<\kappa$, stop the node, since its positive contribution is at most <a id="shift:tiny-node"></a>$$\label{shift:tiny-node}
 e^puv\leq e^p\kappa^{1-\theta}\Phi.$$

Here and throughout this proof, the required scale choices are regular dilates whose logarithmic width losses are polynomial in $p+D$, where $D=\mathop{\mathrm{rank}}B$. Successor ranks are at most $D+(2+p)^{C_\epsilon''}$. To make the set of admissible successor shapes precise, retain $w=w(B)$ and allow all regular presentations $C$ satisfying $$C\subseteq B_{c\zeta/(2+D)},\qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{rank}}C\leq D+(2+p)^{A_\epsilon},\qquad
 w(C)\geq w\exp(-(2+p+D)^{B_\epsilon}).$$ Choose $A_\epsilon$ from <a href="#shift:ap-cost" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:ap-cost">[shift:ap-cost]</a>, which will be applied with $q=O_\epsilon(p^2)$. Choose $B_\epsilon$ after the exponent defining $\zeta$, large enough to cover that almost-periodicity width loss and the bounded number of regular dilations within one refinement. These choices precede peeling. The exponent defining $P$ is chosen last.

*Removing concentration.* While a translate of an admissible $C$ has mean $u_1>Ku$ of $H$, remove the whole slice from $H$. Set $b=|C|/|B|$. The removed contribution is represented, up to $O(e^p\zeta b)$, by nodes of shape $C$ with coefficient $b$: keep the first center fixed, average the second center in its parent cell, and add an independent uniform element of $C$ on that side. This error bound is <a href="#shift:bohr-tv" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:bohr-tv">[shift:bohr-tv]</a>, applied to the second parent cell. The second means average to at most $v$. Consequently their total potential is at most $b(u_1v)^\theta$. Inequality <a href="#shift:peeling" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:peeling">[shift:peeling]</a> pays a factor greater than two for this potential. Perform the same operation if $W$ has such a slice.

Stop immediately if either current mean becomes smaller than $\kappa$. At every other removal, the removed mass is at least $K\kappa b_{\min}>0$, where the volume bound and admissibility give $$b\geq |C|/N\geq b_{\min}:=
 \left(\frac{w\exp(-(2+p+D)^{B_\epsilon})}{10}\right)^{D+(2+p)^{A_\epsilon}}.$$ Thus peeling terminates in finitely many steps. Moreover its errors are summable without multiplying by the number of steps: since $u_1,v\geq\kappa$, each $b$ is at most $\kappa^{-2\theta}b(u_1v)^\theta$, and <a href="#shift:peeling" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:peeling">[shift:peeling]</a> telescopes. It remains to treat a non-tiny remainder for which every admissible translate has $H$-mean at most $Ku$ and $W$-mean at most $Kv$.

*Matching two local scales.* Choose tiny regular dilates $S\ll L\ll B$. Choose $x_0,y_0$ independently and uniformly in the two parent cells, take $r\in L$ and $s=s_1+s_2$ with $s_1,s_2\in S$ independently uniform, and put $$x=x_0+r,\qquad y=y_0-r+s.$$ The resulting average differs from the parent average by $O(e^p\zeta)$, by <a href="#shift:bohr-tv" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:bohr-tv">[shift:bohr-tv]</a> twice. Restrict both weights to $x_0+L$ and $y_0+L$; the further error is $O(e^p\zeta)$ because $s$ is on a much smaller scale than $L$. Let $u_0,v_0$ be the resulting means on $L$. The absence of concentration gives $u_0\leq Ku$, $v_0\leq Kv$; independence of $x_0,y_0$ and concavity give <a id="shift:matched-potential"></a>$$\label{shift:matched-potential}
 \mathbb E_{x_0,y_0}(u_0v_0)^\theta\leq(uv)^\theta.$$

<a id="shift:means-exact"></a>
One can return to independent cells of any sufficiently small common shape $C$ by adding independent $t_1,t_2\in C$ to $x,y$. In $(r,s)$ coordinates this translates the law by $(t_1,t_1+t_2)$, so its total variation changes by $O(\zeta)$. If $U,V$ are the new cell means, then, exactly, $$\label{shift:means-exact}
 \mathbb E_{r,s}U\leq u_0,\quad \mathbb E_{r,s}V\leq v_0,
 \quad \mathbb E_{r,s}(UV)^\theta\leq(u_0v_0)^\theta.$$ For example, for each fixed $s,t_2$, summing the zero-extended second weight over $-L+s+t_2$ is at most its sum over the whole group, namely $|L|v_0$. This proves the second inequality; the first is identical and the last follows by Cauchy–Schwarz and concavity.

If $u_0<c_0u$ or $v_0<c_0v$, return to independent cells in this way. The total potential of these centers is at most $(c_0K)^\theta\Phi\leq\Phi/2$. For the other centers $u_0,v_0\geq c_0\kappa$. Fix one and normalize its truncated weights to functions $F,G$ on $L$ of mean one. Their caps are at most $M=(c_0\kappa)^{-1}$. Choose $m=\lceil c_{\rm mom}p\rceil$ with $c_{\rm mom}=c_{\rm mom}(\epsilon,c_{\rm cut})$ large enough, and apply Lemma <a href="#shift:local-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:local-moments">62</a> with sufficiently small fixed $\delta=\delta(\epsilon)$.

*The flat alternative terminates a matched term.* Its integral, divided by $u_0v_0$, is $\mathbb E_{s\sim\nu_+}a(x_0+y_0+s)(F*G)(s)$. Outside a set of $\nu_+$-measure at most $2^{-2m}$, $|F*G-1|\leq2\delta$. Since $0\leq F*G\leq M$, the exceptional part costs at most $O(e^p(M+1)2^{-2m})$. On the complementary set use $$a(F*G)\leq (1+2\delta)f
              -(1+\epsilon)(1-2\delta)g.$$ Choose $\delta$ so that $(1+\epsilon)(1-2\delta)\geq1+2\delta$.

Hypothesis <a href="#shift:upper-hypothesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:upper-hypothesis">[shift:upper-hypothesis]</a> gives $\mathbb E_{s\sim\nu_+}(f-g)(x_0+y_0+s)\leq\eta$ for any prescribed $\eta=\exp(-(2+p)^{O_\epsilon(1)})$, after taking $P$ sufficiently large. Here is the needed approximation justification. Approximate a translated regular Bohr indicator from above and below by $[0,1]$-valued Lipschitz functions on its defining torus, with transition width $\rho w(S)$. Their difference has normalized group mean at most $O(D\rho)|S|/N$, and their Lipschitz constants are at most $O(D/(\rho w(S)))$. These are degree-one niltests: the torus has lattice $\mathbb Z^D$ and the orbit is given by the defining characters. With $\alpha=|S|/N$, the hypothesis and the signed comparison yield $$\mathbb E_{s\in S}(f-g)(z+s)
 \leq \alpha^{-1}e^{-P}+O(e^pD\rho)
 \qquad(z\in G).$$ The width and rank bookkeeping below bounds both $\log(1/w(S))$ and $\log(1/\alpha)$ polynomially in $p$. Thus $\rho$ can be chosen with polynomial logarithmic loss to make the last display at most $\eta$, with all test complexities at most $P$. Averaging over the second copy of $S$ proves the assertion for $\nu_+$. Thus this node has positive contribution at most an arbitrarily small multiple of $e^{-10p}(u_0v_0)^\theta$.

*The unbalanced alternative contracts the potential.* Let $Q$ be the function supplied by <a href="#shift:unbalanced" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:unbalanced">[shift:unbalanced]</a>, and write $q=2m'=O_\epsilon(p)$. Choose a tiny regular shrink $S'$ of $S$. Regularity, with error small after multiplication by $M^{2q}$, supplies an $s_0\in S$ such that $$\mathbb E_{a\in S,\ b\in s_0+S'}(Q\circ Q)(a-b)^q
 \geq(1+c)^q$$ for a fixed $c>0$. Set $K_0=\{Q\circ Q\geq1+c/2\}\cap(S-s_0-S')$. Regularity gives $|K_0|\leq2|S|$.

For dependent random choice with these real weights, let $L^+$ be a slight dilate of $L$ containing $L-a$ for every $a\in S\cup(s_0+S')$. The scale separation and regularity ensure $|L^+|\leq2|L|$. Independently sample $t_1,\ldots,t_q$ uniformly from $L^+$. Given these samples, include each $a\in S$ in $A_1$, and each $b\in s_0+S'$ in $A_2$, independently, with probabilities $$\prod_{j=1}^q\frac{Q(t_j+a)}{M},\qquad
 \prod_{j=1}^q\frac{Q(t_j+b)}{M}.$$ The expected pair weight is $\bigl(|L|/(|L^+|M^2)\bigr)^q(Q\circ Q)(a-b)^q$. The contribution of pairs outside $K_0$, relative to the lower bound for all pairs, is at most $((1+c/2)/(1+c))^q$. By increasing $m$ by a fixed factor, this is smaller than any chosen fixed constant. To justify the simultaneous density and bad-pair bounds, write $Z=|A_1||A_2|/(|S||S'|)$ and let $Z_{\rm bad}$ be the same normalized count restricted to differences outside $K_0$. The preceding estimates give $\mathbb EZ\ge\exp(-O_\epsilon(p^2))$ and $\mathbb EZ_{\rm bad}\le\delta_*\mathbb EZ$, where $\delta_*$ can be made any sufficiently small fixed constant by increasing the fixed multiple defining $q$. Given a sufficiently large fixed $C_*$, take $C_*\delta_*\le1/2$. Some outcome then has $$Z-C_*Z_{\rm bad}\ge\tfrac12\mathbb EZ.$$ It follows that $Z\ge\exp(-O_\epsilon(p^2))$ and $Z_{\rm bad}/Z\le C_*^{-1}$. Each relative density is at least $Z$, since both are at most one. Thus both densities have the required lower bound and an arbitrarily high fixed fraction of the differences lie in $K_0$.

Apply <a href="#shift:ap-cost" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:ap-cost">[shift:ap-cost]</a> to these sets. Choose a tiny regular shrink $C$ of $D_*$ so that adding independent opposite shifts from $C$ changes the uniform law on $D_*$ by $O(\zeta)$. If $d$ is uniform on $D_*$ and $c_1,c_2$ are independent and uniform on $C$, the almost-periodicity estimate therefore gives $$\mathbb E_{a\in A_1,b\in A_2,d,c_1,c_2}
 1_{K_0}(a-b+d+c_1-c_2)\geq1-\eta_0,$$ where $\eta_0>0$ is any sufficiently small fixed constant. For a finite set $A$, write $\mathsf P_Av(x)=|A|^{-1}\sum_{t\in A}v(x+t)$; these averaging operators do not use the $|L|^{-1}$ normalization of function-function convolution. Since $Q\circ Q\geq1+c/2$ on $K_0$ and is nonnegative everywhere, the last display implies $$\max_x\mathsf P_C\mathsf P_{-C}(Q\circ Q)(x)
 \geq(1+c/2)(1-\eta_0)\geq1+c'$$ for a fixed $c'>0$. This function is the autocorrelation of $\mathsf P_CQ$, with sums normalized by $|L|$. Cauchy–Schwarz puts its maximum at zero. Its mass outside $L$ contributes $O(M^2\zeta)$ to the second moment, so $\mathbb E_{r\in L}(\mathsf P_CQ)(r)^2\geq1+c'/2$. The same estimate holds on the reflected and slightly translated law used by the second weight, by regularity.

Return to independent cells of shape $C$, with centers $x_0+r$ and $y_0-r+s$, where $r$ is uniform on $L$ and $s\sim\nu_+$ independently. Their means satisfy $$U/u_0=\mathsf P_CF(r),\qquad
 V/v_0=\mathsf P_CG(-r+s).$$ This shape is admissible: its rank increase is polynomial in $p$, and its logarithmic width loss relative to $B$ is polynomial in $p+D$, by <a href="#shift:ap-cost" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:ap-cost">[shift:ap-cost]</a> and the intervening regular dilations. The absence of concentration gives $U/u_0,V/v_0\leq K/c_0$. Equations <a href="#shift:means-exact" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:means-exact">[shift:means-exact]</a> give means at most one, and one of these variables has second moment at least $1+c'/4$. Lemma <a href="#shift:potential" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:potential">61</a> therefore contracts the local potential by a fixed factor $q_0<1$.

*Summing the refinements.* Let $A$ be the matched potential from small-ratio centers and $B_1$ that from the other centers. We have $A\leq\Phi/2$ and $A+B_1\leq\Phi$, so the surviving potential is at most $A+q_0B_1\leq(1+q_0)\Phi/2$. For completeness, let $S_{\rm peel}$ be the total weighted potential already extracted by peeling, and $R_{\rm rem}$ the potential of its remainder. Telescoping gives $2S_{\rm peel}+R_{\rm rem}\le\Phi$. The matching argument contracts the surviving remainder potential by $\lambda=(1+q_0)/2<1$; a tiny remainder has no successors. Hence the total successor potential is at most $$S_{\rm peel}+\lambda R_{\rm rem}
 \le\max(1/2,\lambda)\Phi.$$ This gives a fixed $\gamma=\gamma(\epsilon)>0$ such that all successors of a node have total weighted potential at most $(1-\gamma)\Phi$. Their integrals bound its integral from above up to $c_\epsilon e^{-10p}\Phi$, where $c_\epsilon$ can be made arbitrarily small. Indeed all errors before a tiny-mean cutoff are bounded by fixed powers of $e^p\kappa^{-1}$ times $\zeta$; the extracted errors have already been summed by <a href="#shift:peeling" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:peeling">[shift:peeling]</a>.

This proves <a href="#shift:one-round-refinement" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:one-round-refinement">[shift:one-round-refinement]</a> with $\varepsilon_{\rm err}=c_\epsilon e^{-10p}$; admissibility of the successor shapes gives <a href="#shift:one-round-geometry" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:one-round-geometry">[shift:one-round-geometry]</a>.

Apply the refinement for $R=\lceil c_{\rm depth}p\rceil$ rounds. After $r$ rounds, the total weighted potential of the remaining nodes is at most $(1-\gamma)^r\Phi_{\rm root}$. Hence the sum of all refinement errors is at most $\varepsilon_{\rm err}\Phi_{\rm root}/\gamma$, and the remaining positive integral is at most $$e^p(1-\gamma)^R\Phi_{\rm root}.$$ Since $\Phi_{\rm root}\le1$, choosing $c_{\rm depth}$ sufficiently large and then the permitted error constant sufficiently small makes their sum less than $e^{-4p}$.

It remains to justify one comparison budget for the whole refinement. Along every branch, <a href="#shift:one-round-geometry" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:one-round-geometry">[shift:one-round-geometry]</a> gives $$D_{r+1}\le D_r+(2+p)^{A_\epsilon},\qquad
 \log(1/w_{r+1})\le\log(1/w_r)+(2+p+D_r)^{B_\epsilon}.$$ Starting with $D_0=1,w_0=1$, both $D_r$ and $\log(1/w_r)$ are polynomial in $p$ for $r\le R$. The same is true of the intermediate dilates used inside a round. The Bohr volume bound $|B|/N\ge(w(B)/10)^D$ consequently gives a polynomial bound for $\log(N/|B|)$. One choice $P=(2+p)^C$ therefore covers the smooth-test approximations, their required errors, and the size cutoff at every node. This proves the bilinear estimate and, by Lemma <a href="#shift:bilinear" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:bilinear">60</a>, degree-one shift comparison. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-100"></a>
#### The finite-list reduction

For the induction from degree $r$ to degree $r+1$, a violating positive test of degree $r$ may be chosen separately at every shift. We cannot take a union bound over all these tests. Instead we will recover them, on a sufficiently large set of shifts, from two fixed finite lists of positive tests: one observed at $n$, the other at $n+h$. The remaining factor may depend on $h$, but has degree at most $r-1$. Degree-$r$ shift comparison is uniform over this remaining factor, so only the two fixed lists enter the union bound. The next lemma gives the precise reduction. The rest of the proof constructs its factorization.

<a id="stmt-shift-fixed-lists-suffice"></a>
<div id="shift:fixed-lists-suffice" class="lemma">

**Lemma 64** (Why fixed lists suffice). *Assume shift comparison at degree $r\geq1$. Let $0<\epsilon<1$, $0\leq f,g,J\leq e^p$, and suppose that $N$ is odd and $N\geq\exp(P)$ for the sufficiently large polynomial budget $P$ in the conclusion. Suppose, for a set $H\subseteq G$ of density at least $\sigma$, that positive tests $T_h$ satisfy $$\mathbb E_n\bigl(f-(1+\epsilon)g\bigr)(n)J(n+h)T_h(n)>\delta.$$ Suppose there are fixed families $A_i,B_j\in\mathcal T_d(Q)$, $d=r+1$, of sizes at most $F$, and, for each $h\in H$, an approximation $$T_h(n)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}A_{i(\ell,h)}(n)
 B_{j(\ell,h)}(n+h)C_{\ell,h}(n)+e_h(n),
 \qquad C_{\ell,h}\in\mathcal T_{r-1}(Q),$$ with $\mathbb E|e_h|\leq\delta e^{-2p}/6$. Here all factors take values in $[0,1]$. If $$Q+\log(F+M+2)+\log(1/\sigma)+\log(1/\delta)
 \leq(2+p)^{O_{d,\epsilon}(1)},$$ then <a href="#shift:upper-hypothesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:upper-hypothesis">[shift:upper-hypothesis]</a>, with $P$ a sufficiently large polynomial in $p$, rules out these violations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-fixed-lists-suffice"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-fixed-lists-suffice</summary>

*Proof.* Choose $q\geq\max(p,Q)$ polynomially large so that $F^2e^{-q}<\sigma$ and $Me^{-q}<\delta/2$. For each fixed $i,j$, apply degree-$r$ shift comparison to $fA_i,gA_i,JB_j$, with multiplicative slack $\epsilon/2$ and budget $q$. Its hypothesis follows from <a href="#shift:upper-hypothesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:upper-hypothesis">[shift:upper-hypothesis]</a>: multiplying a degree-$r$ test by $A_i$ gives a degree-$d$ positive test, of complexity bounded polynomially in the required budgets. There are at most $F^2$ fixed pairs, so some $h\in H$ lies outside every exceptional set. Uniformity over all lower tests then bounds each summand by $e^{-q}$. Replacing $f-(1+\epsilon/2)g$ by $f-(1+\epsilon)g$ only decreases the integral. Finally $|(f-(1+\epsilon)g)J|\leq3e^{2p}$, so the approximation error costs at most $\delta/2$. This contradicts the displayed violation. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-101"></a>
#### Modeling and a common anchor

To construct the fixed lists, we first approximate each input by a finite linear combination of niltests in a seminorm adapted to the shifted comparisons. The separation argument is a form of the Hahn–Banach method for deriving decompositions from inverse theorems <a id="pm-cite-47"></a>[[GowersHahnBanach2010](#ref-GowersHahnBanach2010), Section 3.2]; the explicit finite list is then obtained by sampling. On a finite probability space, the extended dual of a seminorm $X$ is $$X^*(\psi)=\sup_{X(v)\le1}|\langle v,\psi\rangle|\in[0,\infty].$$ It is finite precisely when $\psi$ annihilates $\ker X$. A family is *balanced* if it is closed under multiplication by complex scalars of modulus at most one.

<a id="stmt-shift-modeling"></a>
<div id="shift:modeling" class="lemma">

**Lemma 65** (Modeling from a seminorm detector). *Let $\Omega$ be a finite probability space, let $X$ be a seminorm on $\mathbb C^\Omega$ with $X(v)\leq K\|v\|_1$, and let $\mathcal S$ be a nonempty compact, balanced collection of functions of supremum at most one. Fix $M,K\geq1$, $\beta>0$, and $0<\tau<1$. Suppose that every $\psi$ satisfying $$\|\psi\|_\infty\leq K/\tau,
 \qquad X(\psi)\geq\tau/M^2$$ has $|\langle\psi,Q\rangle|\geq\beta$ for some $Q\in\mathcal S$. Then every $b$ with $\|b\|_\infty\leq M$ has a representation $$b=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}c_iQ_i+e,\qquad
 \sum_i|c_i|\leq2/\beta,
 \qquad X(e)\leq2\tau,$$ with $\ell\leq1+4K^2/(\beta^2\tau^2)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-modeling"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-modeling</summary>

*Proof.* Write $R=2/\beta$. Suppose that $b$ does not belong to $R\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal S)+\{e:X(e)\leq\tau\}$. Separation in the underlying finite-dimensional real vector space gives a nonzero $\psi$ with $$\operatorname{Re}\langle b,\psi\rangle>
 R\sup_{Q\in\mathcal S}|\langle Q,\psi\rangle|
 +\tau X^*(\psi).$$ The right side is positive; normalize it to one. Then $X^*(\psi)\leq1/\tau$. Since $X(v)\leq K\|v\|_1$, testing on point masses yields $\|\psi\|_\infty\leq K/\tau$. Also $\|\psi\|_2>1/M$, by the strict lower bound on $\operatorname{Re}\langle b,\psi\rangle$. Duality gives $X(\psi)X^*(\psi)\geq\|\psi\|_2^2$ and consequently $X(\psi)>\tau/M^2$. The detection hypothesis contradicts $R\sup_Q|\langle Q,\psi\rangle|\leq1$. The indicated convex sum therefore exists with $X(e)\leq\tau$. Its structural part has $\ell^1$ coefficient norm at most $R$. Sample $\ell$ independent terms with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes, absorbing their phases into $\mathcal S$. The expected squared $L^2$ error of the empirical average is at most $R^2/\ell$. Take $\ell\geq R^2K^2/\tau^2$ and use $X\leq K\|\cdot\|_2$. ◻

</details>

<a id="shift:testing-seminorm"></a>
<a id="shift:detector-cs"></a>
In the application to shift comparison, $$\label{shift:testing-seminorm}
 X(e)=\mathbb E_h\sup_L
 \left|\mathbb E_ne(n)B(n+h)L(n)\right|,$$ where $L$ ranges over complex, unit-bounded degree-$r$ niltests of controlled complexity and all their cyclic translates. Thus the family includes $n\mapsto L_0(n+t)$, with addition taken in $G$, even when its representative path wraps. The supremum allows a different test and translation at each $h$. It is a seminorm and $X(e)\leq\|B\|_\infty\|e\|_1$. Choosing an approximately maximizing test and aligning its phase, then applying Cauchy–Schwarz at $n+h$, gives $$\label{shift:detector-cs}
 X(e)^2\leq\|B\|_\infty^2
 \mathbb E_{h,k}\left|
 \mathbb E_n e(n)\overline{e(n+h-k)}
 L_h(n)\overline{L_k(n+h-k)}\right|.$$ The product in <a href="#shift:detector-cs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="shift:detector-cs">[shift:detector-cs]</a> contains at most two translated representative niltests. Lemma <a href="#prelim:dual-gowers" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:dual-gowers">55</a> therefore applies uniformly, and the derivative identity gives a quantitative $U^{r+2}$ detector. The quasipolynomial inverse theorem <a id="pm-cite-48"></a>[[LSSInverse2024](#ref-LSSInverse2024)] then supplies the structural tests for Lemma <a href="#shift:modeling" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:modeling">65</a>. These structural tests are ordinary degree-$(r+1)$ niltests; only the testing family has been enlarged. The translated family permits the change of variable $m=n+h$ when modeling the second input: $L_h(n)$ becomes $L_h(m-h)$. The supremum handles these translations directly, without a union bound over them. All cutoff errors in the converse estimate are chosen below the detection threshold.

<a id="stmt-shift-anchor"></a>
<div id="shift:anchor" class="lemma">

**Lemma 66** (A common anchor). *Let $H$ be a finite nonempty set. For $1\leq j\leq m$ and $h\in H$, let $v_{h,j}$ be complex functions of supremum at most one on finite probability spaces $\Omega_j$. Suppose $|\mathbb Ev_{h,j}|\geq\delta>0$ for all $h,j$. There exist $h_0\in H$ and $H'\subseteq H$ with $|H'|\geq\delta^{2m}|H|/2$ such that $$|\mathbb Ev_{h,j}\overline{v_{h_0,j}}|
 \geq\delta^{2m}/2\qquad(h\in H',\ 1\leq j\leq m).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-anchor"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-anchor</summary>

*Proof.* Multiply each $v_{h,j}$ by a unit scalar so its mean is real and nonnegative, and tensor the functions in their independent variables to form $V_h$ on $\prod_j\Omega_j$. Then $\mathbb EV_h\geq\delta^m$ and $\|V_h\|_2\leq1$. Consequently $$\mathbb E_{h,k}\operatorname{Re}\langle V_h,V_k\rangle
 =\|\mathbb E_hV_h\|_2^2\geq\delta^{2m}.$$ Choose $h_0$ with the same lower bound after averaging only $h$. At least a $\delta^{2m}/2$ fraction have real inner product at least $\delta^{2m}/2$. For these $h$, the absolute inner product is a product of $m$ numbers in $[0,1]$, so each factor is at least $\delta^{2m}/2$. Removing the aligning phases changes no absolute value. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-102"></a>
#### Recovering tests from two fixed observations

The next lemma records precisely what positive discretization can do after the requisite geometry has been established.

<a id="stmt-shift-discretization"></a>
<div id="shift:discretization" class="lemma">

**Lemma 67** (Positive discretization). *Fix finite families of nonnegative functions $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ and $\{B_j\}_{j\in J}$ on $G$, each summing to one. For each shift $h$, suppose that, outside a set $E_h$, $$T_h(n)=F_h(z_h(n),\xi_h(n)),$$ where $0\leq F_h\leq1$ and $F_h$ is $L$-Lipschitz in its second variable. Suppose that whenever $A_i(n)B_j(n+h)$ and $A_i(n')B_j(n'+h)$ are positive, with $n,n'\notin E_h$, one has $d(\xi_h(n),\xi_h(n'))\leq\rho$. Then there are functions $C_{ij,h}(n)=F_h(z_h(n),\xi_{ij,h})$ such that <a id="shift:positive-discretization"></a>$$\label{shift:positive-discretization}
 \left|T_h(n)-\sum_{i,j}A_i(n)B_j(n+h)C_{ij,h}(n)\right|
 \leq L\rho\quad(n\notin E_h).$$ An empty cell pair may be assigned $C_{ij,h}=0$. If the first-variable sections of $F_h$ are bounded Lipschitz functions on a degree-$(r-1)$ nilmanifold and $z_h$ is a polynomial path on it, then every $C_{ij,h}$ is a degree-$(r-1)$ niltest with the corresponding uniform complexity.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-discretization"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-discretization</summary>

*Proof.* For every nonempty cell pair select a point $n_{ij,h}\notin E_h$ where its weight is positive and put $\xi_{ij,h}=\xi_h(n_{ij,h})$. For each contributing pair the replacement error is at most $L\rho$. Sum against the nonnegative weights, whose sum is one. The final assertion follows by restricting $F_h$ to the chosen second coordinate. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-shift-uniform-cover"></a>
<div id="shift:uniform-cover" class="lemma">

**Lemma 68** (Uniform recovery after right normalization). *Fix controlled rational nilpotent groups, lattices, and a rational subgroup $V$ of their product. Fix a controlled lattice $\Lambda_V$ on $V$. There are fixed fine covers of the input lattices with the following property. Fix bounded left translations and arbitrary right translations by elements of the original input lattices, and apply these same translations to both of two tuples. Suppose that both normalized tuples belong to $V$. If the two original tuples are within $\rho$ on the fixed input covers, then their normalized images are within $\mathcal B(p)\rho$ on $V/\Lambda_V$, provided $\rho\leq\mathcal B(p)^{-1}$. The covers and constants do not depend on the right translations. The left translations may instead differ by at most $\rho$ in each coordinate; the same conclusion holds after enlarging its constant. One may additionally require compatibility with right translation by rational elements having a fixed common denominator $q\leq\mathcal B(p)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-uniform-cover"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-uniform-cover</summary>

*Proof.* First choose a fine ambient product lattice $\Lambda_0$ such that $V\cap\Lambda_0\subseteq\Lambda_V$. The restriction of the ambient quotient metric has a controlled local inverse on $V/(V\cap\Lambda_0)$. To see this directly, reduce both points using $V\cap\Lambda_0$ to bounded representatives. An ambient lattice element witnessing closeness is then bounded. Its logarithm lies in a controlled rational grid; if its distance from the rational subspace $\log V$ is below the rational separation bound, it lies in that subspace exactly. It therefore belongs to $V\cap\Lambda_0$. Controlled coordinate changes compare the ambient and intrinsic small distances. This is also the metric argument in Lemma <a href="#prelim:reconstruction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:reconstruction">49</a>.

Choose each input cover $\Lambda$ inside the corresponding factor of $\Lambda_0$, normal in the original lattice $\Gamma$. Here is an explicit construction. If $\log\Gamma\subseteq l^{-1}\mathbb Z^D$ and $m_0\mathbb Z^D\subseteq\log\Lambda_0$, choose a controlled integer $m$ divisible by $lm_0$, and set $$\Lambda=\langle\gamma^m:\gamma\in\Gamma\rangle.$$ Every generator lies in $\Lambda_0$ because $\log(\gamma^m)=m\log\gamma\in m_0\mathbb Z^D$. This subgroup is characteristic in $\Gamma$. A Mal’cev normal form with $D$ coordinates gives $[\Gamma:\Lambda]\leq m^D$ by reducing each exponent modulo $m$; powers of the Mal’cev generators give controlled grids for $\Lambda$. Thus all logarithmic index and coordinate costs remain polynomial.

For one coordinate, let $a=\epsilon^{-1}x\gamma^{-1}$ and $a'=\epsilon^{-1}x'\gamma^{-1}$, with $\epsilon$ bounded and $\gamma\in\Gamma$. If $d_G(x\lambda,x')\leq\rho$ for $\lambda\in\Lambda$, then $$a(\gamma\lambda\gamma^{-1})
   =\epsilon^{-1}x\lambda\gamma^{-1},\qquad
 d_G\bigl(a(\gamma\lambda\gamma^{-1}),a'\bigr)
   \leq\mathop{\mathrm{Lip}}(L_{\epsilon^{-1}})\rho.$$ Normality puts $\gamma\lambda\gamma^{-1}$ in $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda_0$. Thus normalized ambient distances are controlled uniformly in $\gamma$. Apply the preceding local inverse on $V$. If the bounded left normalizers are $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon'$, right invariance gives $$d_G(\epsilon^{-1}x'\gamma^{-1},
       (\epsilon')^{-1}x'\gamma^{-1})
 =d_G(\epsilon^{-1},(\epsilon')^{-1}).$$ Inversion is controlled on the bounded set of normalizers, so their variation adds at most $\mathcal B(p)\rho$ before applying the local inverse. No orbit representative enters this error bound.

For rational right translations, the adjoint formula has a common denominator bounded in terms of $q$ and the structural data; its numerators need not be bounded. Choose the earlier congruence strides sufficiently divisible to force the required conjugates into $\Lambda_0$. This requires no bound on those numerators. Again normal refinement inside $\Gamma$ handles arbitrary lattice right translations at the same time. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-shift-higher"></a>
<div id="shift:higher" class="proposition">

**Proposition 69** (Higher-degree propagation). *Lemmas  <a href="#prelim:reconstruction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:reconstruction">49</a>, <a href="#prelim:symbol-splitting" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:symbol-splitting">52</a>, <a href="#prelim:square" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:square">54</a>, <a href="#prelim:dual-gowers" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:dual-gowers">55</a>, and <a href="#prelim:step-drop" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prelim:step-drop">56</a>, together with the quasipolynomial inverse theorem, imply the propagation principle in Theorem <a href="#shift:required" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:required">58</a> for every fixed degree.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-shift-higher"><summary>Proof of stmt-shift-higher</summary>

*Proof.* Induct on $d$, using Proposition <a href="#shift:degree-one" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="shift:degree-one">63</a> for the base case. Set $r=d-1\geq1$ and $a=f-(1+\epsilon)g$. Suppose that a set of more than $e^{-p}N$ shifts has a violating positive degree-$r$ test $T_h$.
